blueprints.proposed: A shared document layer where each paragraph has a permanent address, links carry a type, and any reader can set a viewspec to see the whole at the resolution they need.
blueprints.originality: Engelbart treated documents as structured, interoperable working environments, with links to individual objects and adjustable views.

origin.title: Knowledge-Domain Interoperability and an Open Hyperdocument System
origin.summary: Engelbart proposed a common document infrastructure spanning organizations and software vendors. Documents would contain individually addressable objects, support different views of the same material, and expose incoming links. His concern was the continuity of collective knowledge: a decision, its evidence, and later revisions should remain connected when people change tools or work across organizational boundaries.

history.summary: AUGMENT and HyperScope implemented parts of the OHS vision. Shared document addressing and views across independent tools remain the direction to explore.
history.whatWasBuilt: The 1990 paper explicitly draws on AUGMENT and workplace pilots. HyperScope later reproduced selected navigation and viewing capabilities in a browser: paragraph addresses, adjustable outlines, and links that encode a chosen view. It used OPML and was presented by its creators as an initial step toward OHS.
history.whatRemains: Build a small environment for reviewing specifications across tools: the same passage can be cited from a discussion, inspected alongside its history, and opened in another compatible reader. Start by testing that workflow across two independent tools.

whyNow.summary: Our proposed benefit is easier handover in volunteer technical projects. A new contributor could follow a decision to the exact requirement and evidence instead of reconstructing context from several documents. HyperScope supplies a concrete interface and format to study; the community still needs to test whether durable references improve real review work.
beneficiaries: Open-source maintainers explaining long-lived design decisions
Standards and civic-technology groups reviewing complex proposals
New contributors joining a project after its initial discussions

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Two independently implemented readers exchange a 100-paragraph specification and preserve citations while authors reorganize it.

steps.title: Define what an address promises
steps.description: Distinguish a stable object identifier from its current outline position. Specify what happens after a move, split, deletion, or revision; retain a tombstone and previous version when a cited object disappears.
steps.deliverable: A small document format, address rules, and an annotated example specification.

steps.title: Build two views of one document
steps.description: Implement an outline reader and a review reader against the same exported data. Include keyboard navigation and a way to expand cited passages without losing surrounding context.
steps.deliverable: Two working readers and an interoperability fixture set.

steps.title: Connect decisions to evidence
steps.description: Let reviewers attach a reason and a typed relationship to a passage. Show incoming references and distinguish a quotation of a historical revision from a link to the current text.
steps.deliverable: A review session with requirements, objections, and decision links.

steps.title: Run a handover study
steps.description: Ask contributors unfamiliar with the specification to recover the reasons behind five changes. Compare completion time and interpretation errors with a normal linked document, then publish the anonymized results.
steps.deliverable: A reproducible comparison and prioritized usability findings.

successCriteria: All 30 preselected citations remain resolvable or explicitly marked deleted after 50 structural edits and export/import through both readers.
At least four of five new reviewers correctly identify the evidence behind four of five sampled decisions.
Keyboard-only participants can open, inspect, and return from a citation without losing their reading position.
nonGoals: Rebuilding all of NLS/AUGMENT or replacing every project tool
Claiming permanent availability for content the group does not control

blueprints.proposed: Quote by pointing at the original rather than copying. The included passage remains live, attributed and traceable to its origin.

origin.title: Evolutionary documents and transclusion
origin.summary: Nelson's 1965 paper proposed a file structure for changing personal documents and unresolved alternatives. His later xanalogical model made shared content and its origins visible across documents and versions. Transclusion is more than inserting a remote fragment: readers should be able to recognize the reused material and inspect its relationship to the source.

history.summary: Transclusion has been implemented. The opportunity is to carry its provenance-preserving behavior into a focused, usable collaboration tool.
history.whatWasBuilt: The Udanax Green release contains a C backend and a Python front end for viewing and editing documents, with known bugs documented by its authors. Nelson and collaborators also demonstrated links and transclusions in XanaduSpace.
history.whatRemains: Build an evidence notebook in which a research group assembles an argument from permitted source passages, compares the original context beside each quotation, and receives an explicit choice when a source changes. Treat exact-version citations and intentionally updating inclusions as different user actions.

whyNow.summary: Our hypothesis is that groups writing explainers, technical proposals, or community research could avoid context loss if quotations remained connected to the exact material they used. Nelson's model supplies the provenance concept. The proposed benefit must be tested with readers; preserving a connection does not itself establish that the source is trustworthy or that an argument is sound.
beneficiaries: Community researchers assembling evidence from several documents
Technical writers maintaining explanations across changing specifications
Readers checking whether a quotation supports a claim

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Publish one jointly written explainer using 20 reusable passages from ten permission-cleared documents, with every passage traceable to its exact source version.

steps.title: Make an explicit source record
steps.description: Store source location, revision identity, selected span, surrounding context, and reuse permission. Begin with team-authored or openly licensed text so the prototype has a small, auditable corpus.
steps.deliverable: A source registry and portable document package.

steps.title: Compose with visible provenance
steps.description: Let writers include a passage by reference and inspect the source alongside the draft. Clearly separate the original words from commentary, omissions, and edited paraphrases.
steps.deliverable: A two-pane editor with source-linked excerpts and readable export.

steps.title: Handle change without rewriting history
steps.description: Keep the version originally cited, detect available updates, and let a reviewer accept or reject each replacement. When retrieval fails, label the retained snapshot rather than presenting it as a live original.
steps.deliverable: An update review flow covering changes, deletion, and unavailable sources.

steps.title: Test whether readers recover context
steps.description: Give readers deliberate examples of misleading omissions and changed definitions. Compare how reliably they identify the problem using connected passages versus ordinary copied quotations.
steps.deliverable: A small reader study and a public set of provenance edge cases.

successCriteria: Every displayed excerpt resolves to its stored source revision after the original is edited or moved.
Five independent readers can locate the surrounding context of at least 18 of 20 excerpts within two actions each.
No source update changes the published explainer without a recorded review decision.
nonGoals: Recreating a universal publishing or micropayment network
Granting reuse rights to third-party text merely because it can be linked or retrieved

blueprints.name: A notebook that reunites after a week offline
blueprints.line: Collect observations together even when nobody has a reliable connection.
blueprints.proposed: Build a fieldwork notebook where three people collect observations offline for seven days, then merge their notes with a clear explanation of conflicting edits and authorship.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a fieldwork notebook where three people collect observations offline for seven days, then merge their notes with a clear explanation of conflicting edits and authorship.
blueprints.existingWork: Automerge already provides conflict-free data structures, persistence, and a synchronization protocol for local-first applications. This experiment focuses on understandable reconciliation and recovery for a fieldwork team.

origin.title: Local-first software: collaboration with a usable local copy
origin.summary: The local-first research agenda argues that collaboration need not make a remote service the sole keeper of a user's work. Its authors proposed applications that remain useful offline, synchronize across devices, and preserve long-term user control. Their prototypes explored conflict-free replicated data types as one technical foundation for combining those properties.

history.summary: Local-first collaboration is an implemented approach. This entry proposes a fieldwork workflow whose recovery and reconciliation behavior can be understood by people collecting observations.
history.whatWasBuilt: Automerge stores independently editable document copies, synchronizes changes, retains history, and supports branching and merging. Its conflict API can expose competing property values instead of hiding them behind the default visible value. That machinery provides consistency, but the application still has to explain what conflicting observations mean.
history.whatRemains: The proposed notebook should distinguish a new observation from a correction to an existing one, preserve attribution, and show which device has backed up which records. After a week apart, a team should reconcile conflicting labels or counts without mistaking automatic convergence for agreement about the field evidence.

whyNow.summary: Our proposed use is a small ecological survey or community infrastructure audit where connectivity cannot be assumed. Automerge already supplies synchronization and local histories, letting a team concentrate on confidence, recovery, and a usable handover. Whether this improves fieldwork is a hypothesis to test with an actual group and its existing record-keeping practice.
beneficiaries: Field researchers collecting observations away from reliable networks

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Three collectors record and edit 100 observations over seven offline days, then reconcile their copies and recover from one deliberately lost device.

steps.title: Model evidence separately from interpretation
steps.description: Give observations stable identifiers and append corrections with attribution. Keep a measured value, its units, an observer's interpretation, and optional attachments separate so a changed label cannot silently replace the underlying evidence.
steps.deliverable: An observation schema and realistic, permission-cleared sample survey.

steps.title: Make offline confidence visible
steps.description: Provide an explicit local-save indicator, a pending-transfer count, and export to an ordinary file. Show which observations exist only on this device and explain what a backup actually contains.
steps.deliverable: A notebook that restarts offline and exports a recoverable package.

steps.title: Design the reunion
steps.description: Group concurrent changes by observation. Show conflicting values and their authors, allow both accounts to remain, and record a later reconciliation as a new decision rather than deleting its alternatives.
steps.deliverable: A reconciliation screen with conflict, duplicate, and attachment cases.

steps.title: Rehearse failure with collectors
steps.description: Run the seven-day exercise with interrupted transfers, clock differences, and a device removed after backup. Ask collectors to explain what was recovered, what is still uncertain, and whose records need another copy.
steps.deliverable: A loss report, usability observations, and a recovery runbook.

successCriteria: All acknowledged observations with a second copy survive the simulated device loss; any records that lacked a second copy are explicitly identified.
The three replicas converge after transfers are repeated in different orders, with all 12 seeded disagreements still inspectable.
Each collector correctly identifies whether a sample observation is saved locally, backed up, or awaiting another person's review.
nonGoals: Guaranteeing recovery of information that existed only on a lost device
Providing scientific validation or automatic resolution of contradictory observations

blueprints.name: Software that survives its own data format
blueprints.line: Let collaborators customize their tools without losing the ability to exchange information.
blueprints.proposed: Connect three independently evolving project trackers through reversible schema translations. Let a team rename or split fields without requiring every collaborator to upgrade at once.
blueprints.opportunity: Connect three independently evolving project trackers through reversible schema translations. Let a team rename or split fields without requiring every collaborator to upgrade at once.
blueprints.existingWork: Cambria already implements bidirectional schema lenses and was used in an experimental issue tracker. Its repository describes it as immature software. This proposal tests compatibility across tools that different teams customize independently.

origin.title: Project Cambria: Translate your data with lenses
origin.summary: Cambria explored a translation layer between evolving data schemas. Developers describe a change with a bidirectional lens, allowing related versions of an application to exchange documents and edits. The larger ambition was software that people could customize independently while continuing to collaborate, including communities without one authority deciding everybody's data format.

history.summary: The research included a working library and an issue-tracker experiment. A community continuation could explore how people understand compatibility between tools with different data formats.
history.whatWasBuilt: Cambria translates JSON documents, patches, and schema descriptions. Its researchers demonstrated issue-tracker clients using different schema versions together, but documented limitations such as translating multiple assignees into a single-assignee view. The repository describes the library as immature rather than production-ready.
history.whatRemains: Build three independently customized project trackers: one uses a simple completed flag, one tracks stages, and one adds community-specific review fields. Each team should see what another tool cannot represent, keep hidden information recoverable, and decide when a translation is no longer good enough.

whyNow.summary: Our proposal is to make customization affordable for small organizations sharing work without sharing identical processes. The existing research provides a testable translation mechanism and examples of its limits. A community experiment could establish which kinds of format divergence are worth supporting, instead of assuming that unrestricted customization always improves collaboration.
beneficiaries: Volunteer organizations coordinating across different project trackers
Maintainers supporting old and new application versions
Teams adapting shared software to local terminology

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Three small trackers exchange 200 tasks and updates through five schema changes, with documented treatment of every value a destination cannot display.

steps.title: Define a compatibility contract
steps.description: List the shared meanings of status, assignee, review, and deletion. Write examples where representations differ, including a multi-assignee task viewed by a tool that permits one person.
steps.deliverable: Three schemas, representative records, and an explicit information-preservation policy.

steps.title: Build and explain the translations
steps.description: Implement a small graph of lenses for renames, defaults, enumerated values, and nested fields. Show users the path taken and a concise list of information absent from their current view.
steps.deliverable: A translator with inspectable before-and-after examples.

steps.title: Keep updates reversible where possible
steps.description: Retain the richer source record while applying edits from a simpler client. Mark irreducibly ambiguous changes for review and distinguish unsupported fields from intentionally deleted values.
steps.deliverable: An update bridge with loss reports and a reconciliation queue.

steps.title: Let teams diverge deliberately
steps.description: Ask three groups to change their tracker independently during a two-week trial. Run delayed and reordered updates through every client, then document where shared vocabulary or an upgrade was preferable to another translation.
steps.deliverable: An interoperability report and a reusable compatibility test corpus.

successCriteria: After 1,000 replayed updates, no value disappears without a corresponding explicit deletion or recorded translation limitation.
All clients can read the shared subset after each of five schema changes without a coordinated upgrade.
At least four of five reviewers correctly predict the result of each lossy example using the displayed translation explanation.
nonGoals: Automatically inferring that two similarly named fields mean the same thing
Promising lossless translation between arbitrary schemas

blueprints.name: Living diagrams that explain their assumptions
blueprints.line: Turn a model into something people can manipulate, question, and explain together.
blueprints.proposed: Build a diagram editor where a group can manipulate a model, inspect the assumptions behind each formula, compare alternatives, and publish a portable interactive explanation.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a diagram editor where a group can manipulate a model, inspect the assumptions behind each formula, compare alternatives, and publish a portable interactive explanation.
blueprints.existingWork: Apparatus already combines graphics editing and programming to create interactive diagrams. This experiment adds inspectable assumptions, alternative models, and a review workflow for teams.

origin.title: Apparatus and diagrams as a medium for thinking
origin.summary: Apparatus joined a drawing interface to a dataflow programming environment. In his 2015 presentation, Schachman argued that interactive diagrams could communicate relationships and causality while also helping authors develop their own understanding. He wanted the transition from exploring a diagram to modifying it to feel continuous, without repeatedly translating spatial ideas into drawing code.

history.summary: Apparatus demonstrated a working editor for interactive diagrams and influenced the later commercial design tool Cuttle. The proposed continuation adds shared evidence and review to that editing model.
history.whatWasBuilt: The browser editor includes expressions, manipulable graphics, examples, and tutorials. Published demonstrations include geometry, tides, and mechanical relationships. Its repository provides the implementation under MIT terms.
history.whatRemains: Build a reviewable layer around each model: where an input came from, which simplifying assumptions it encodes, when the model stops applying, and what changes under another interpretation. Test whether this helps a group inspect and revise a shared explanation.

whyNow.summary: A useful first community could be a repair cooperative comparing spare-parts inventory policies. Our hypothesis is that a shared diagram with visible assumptions would make disagreement more productive than comparing unexplained totals. The existing editor provides a concrete starting point; the community can spend its effort on comprehensibility, evidence, and review rather than inventing a graphics engine.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Publish one portable inventory model whose five inputs each have units, a source or explicit estimate, an explanation, and an editable range.

steps.title: Model one real decision
steps.description: Work with a cooperative to define a restocking question. Implement two competing assumptions about repair demand, label invented example data, and document what the model deliberately leaves out.
steps.deliverable: A runnable diagram and a short decision brief.

steps.title: Make reasoning inspectable
steps.description: Connect every output to its dependencies. Let readers select an assumption, inspect its evidence, change its value, and compare the resulting alternatives side by side.
steps.deliverable: An assumption inspector and saved scenario comparison.

steps.title: Review and publish
steps.description: Allow a reviewer to propose a changed assumption with a reason. Export the accepted version with its model, sources, and interaction code, then test it on a fresh device.
steps.deliverable: A versioned example that works without the author's account.

successCriteria: Four of five first-time readers correctly identify which assumption caused an output difference.
Every numeric output can be traced to its formula and documented inputs.
An exported scenario reproduces the same results on a second browser.
nonGoals: Certifying that a model predicts real outcomes.
A general simulation suite or replacement for specialist engineering tools.

blueprints.name: A personal web repair kit
blueprints.line: Reshape a website around your own needs and share the adaptation with others.
blueprints.proposed: Let someone reorganize a difficult website using a spreadsheet view, save the adaptation locally, and share a recipe that explains the browser permissions it needs.
blueprints.opportunity: Let someone reorganize a difficult website using a spreadsheet view, save the adaptation locally, and share a recipe that explains the browser permissions it needs.
blueprints.existingWork: Wildcard already explores website customization through tabular views and browser extensions. Its repository describes prerelease software with incomplete features. This experiment focuses on adaptations that people can inspect, maintain, and share.

origin.title: Wildcard's spreadsheet-driven website customization
origin.summary: Wildcard investigated whether people could adapt existing websites through a synchronized table. Programmers supplied adapters that exposed a site's data; users could then sort, filter, annotate, or combine that data. The research separated the work of maintaining an adapter from the everyday act of changing a website to suit a personal need.

history.summary: Wildcard demonstrated website customization through a synchronized table. Its authors identified adapter maintenance and broader use as open research questions.
history.whatWasBuilt: Demonstrations included sorting listings, adding private annotations, enriching results with another data source, and making a task list support snoozing. The project exposes source code and development installation instructions.
history.whatRemains: Develop a dependable library of local adaptations for a small set of cooperating sites, with understandable permissions, regression examples, and an easy way to report a broken recipe. The proposed contribution is the maintenance and trust workflow around customization.

whyNow.summary: Our proposed pilot pairs a library or community organization with members who struggle to compare information on its website. A shared adaptation could reduce repetitive work while providing concrete evidence for the site's own maintainers. Starting with cooperating sites also makes updates and evaluation practical. Whether people find this easier than asking for a native website change is a question for the pilot.
beneficiaries: People who need alternative ways to organize web information
Website maintainers learning from repeated usability problems

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Ship three reversible, locally stored adaptations for one consenting partner site: sorting a list, hiding irrelevant rows, and adding private notes.

steps.title: Choose a narrow repair
steps.description: Observe five people completing a repeated task. Agree on the information to expose and create test pages with representative content, including missing values and changed layouts.
steps.deliverable: A task brief, a site adapter, and reproducible page fixtures.

steps.title: Package an inspectable recipe
steps.description: Record the exact sites and fields a recipe needs. Show a preview, store notes separately from shared recipes, and provide one-action disable and reset controls.
steps.deliverable: A recipe format with a permission summary and working undo.

steps.title: Build shared maintenance
steps.description: Run adapters against the fixtures on every change. Let users attach a redacted failure report and pin a known version until they choose an update.
steps.deliverable: A small recipe directory with compatibility results and repair instructions.

successCriteria: Four of five participants complete the chosen task without help after a short introduction.
Sharing a recipe never includes personal annotations or page content.
Every tested website change either passes the fixtures or produces an explicit unsupported-state message.
nonGoals: Bypassing logins, paywalls, or website access restrictions.
Automatic support for arbitrary websites or a claim of universal accessibility.

challenges.title: Local changes versus remote actions

blueprints.name: A workspace whose tools members can reshape
blueprints.line: Give a group room to change the software they use while they are using it.
blueprints.proposed: Build a workspace where a member can change a board or calculator directly, submit the change for review, and restore an earlier version without leaving the workspace.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a workspace where a member can change a board or calculator directly, submit the change for review, and restore an earlier version without leaving the workspace.
blueprints.existingWork: lively.next already combines live programming, direct manipulation, and collaboration, and is developed as beta software. This proposal explores review and recovery when a group changes its everyday tools.

origin.title: Lively Kernel's self-modifying browser environment
people: Sun Microsystems Laboratories Lively Kernel team
origin.summary: The Lively Kernel technical overview described a browser environment that contained its own tools for making and changing applications. Its central ambition was to let people alter running software from within that software, using graphical manipulation alongside programming. The environment could export created objects and applications rather than requiring an external development toolchain for every change.

history.summary: Lively Kernel combined live coding and graphical editing in a working browser environment. lively.next continues that work with collaboration and a personal programming kit; this proposal focuses on reviewing changes to shared tools.
history.whatWasBuilt: The original system included graphical objects, an inspector, a code browser, and editing tools. The present lively.next repository supplies an extensible implementation, while warning that it remains beta software with changing APIs.
history.whatRemains: Make tool changes understandable and recoverable for a small group whose everyday work depends on them. The specific experiment is a review process for changing a shared board or calculator while preserving both its records and a known working version.

whyNow.summary: A volunteer workshop could use this approach to adapt its equipment booking board as local practices change. Our hypothesis is that members will make useful improvements when experimentation is separated from the shared working version and recovery is obvious. The existing implementation lets a community concentrate on that social workflow. The experiment should measure maintenance burden as carefully as the number of customizations made.
beneficiaries: Small teams that want control over their own tools

buildPlan.firstMilestone: A five-person workshop uses one booking board, proposes a changed booking rule, reviews it, and restores the previous behavior without losing bookings.

steps.title: Separate records and behavior
steps.description: Build a minimal board with stable booking identifiers and explicit rule versions. Document which edits affect presentation, validation, or stored data so later recovery has a clear meaning.
steps.deliverable: A working board with exportable records and three example rules.

steps.title: Make a change reviewable
steps.description: Give members a private trial copy using sample records. Show a before-and-after example for every proposed rule change, and require an authorized member to adopt it for the group.
steps.deliverable: A proposal screen with behavior examples and attribution.

steps.title: Rehearse recovery
steps.description: Introduce an intentionally broken rule and a conflicting change. Practice rejecting, correcting, and restoring behavior, then repeat with a member who did not develop the board.
steps.deliverable: A recovery demonstration and a short guide the group can follow.

successCriteria: A member without programming experience can explain a proposed rule change from its examples.
Restoring the previous rule preserves all valid bookings created since the change.
Two non-author members successfully perform recovery in under five minutes.
nonGoals: Replacing the group's entire operating system or office suite.
Allowing arbitrary unreviewed code to execute with shared credentials.

roles.contribution: Supplies real booking rules and tests how changes affect work.

challenges.title: Shared authority

blueprints.name: A project passport you can take between communities
blueprints.line: Keep your project profile and contribution record when you move to a different community.
blueprints.proposed: Store a builder's project profile and contribution records in their own data space. Demonstrate moving between two community applications without recreating the information or granting both applications permanent access.
blueprints.opportunity: Store a builder's project profile and contribution records in their own data space. Demonstrate moving between two community applications without recreating the information or granting both applications permanent access.
blueprints.existingWork: Community Solid Server already provides Solid Pods, identity, and modular personal storage. This experiment applies that foundation to portable community participation and understandable permissions.

origin.title: Solid and the decentralized social Web
origin.summary: The Solid demonstration described social applications working on personal data stored independently of the applications themselves. A person could choose a data provider and use multiple applications over the same information. An earlier 2008 proposal from the Southampton and MIT researchers explored this separation for profiles, relationships, access control, and activity streams.

history.summary: Personal data stores and Solid applications already exist. The proposed continuation is a portable record of community participation with understandable sharing and provenance.
history.whatWasBuilt: Community Solid Server implements Pods, identity, persistence options, and configurable server components. The Solid Protocol describes how applications read and write externally stored resources with authentication and authorization; its published report explicitly identifies itself as a Community Group specification, not a W3C Standard.
history.whatRemains: A builder should be able to bring a project profile and selected contributions to a second community without re-entering them or automatically exposing every past affiliation. The application must distinguish a person's own claims from statements confirmed by a project, and make changes in sharing visible.

whyNow.summary: Our proposed benefit is continuity for people whose useful work spans several small communities. A portable profile could preserve a person's chosen project context while leaving each community free to set its own membership rules. Existing server and protocol implementations allow a focused trial; they do not prove that users will want portable participation records or understand the permissions without careful design.
beneficiaries: Builders contributing to several open-source communities
Volunteer groups whose membership changes over time
People wishing to share selected work without a universal public profile

buildPlan.firstMilestone: A builder moves a profile and ten selected contribution records between two independent community applications, then revokes the first application's future access.

steps.title: Agree on a small participation vocabulary
steps.description: Describe projects, roles, contribution links, dates, and who made each claim. Keep private affiliations and public work in separate resources. Make optional fields genuinely optional rather than inventing a universal reputation score.
steps.deliverable: A documented data shape and synthetic profiles covering different sharing choices.

steps.title: Build two independent clients
steps.description: Have one client edit a profile and another render a portfolio from the same permitted data. The second client must discover supported fields without relying on the first application's private database.
steps.deliverable: Two clients and a self-hosted test Pod.

steps.title: Explain and withdraw access
steps.description: Show the exact records and operations requested before granting access. Demonstrate revocation of future reads and writes, and explain that information already downloaded cannot be recalled by changing a permission.
steps.deliverable: A sharing review, revocation flow, and recorded access checks.

steps.title: Rehearse a community transition
steps.description: Ask contributors to choose which records to bring to a new group. Include a withdrawn claim, a renamed project, and an unavailable confirmation source; observe where the receiving community needs context rather than automatic trust.
steps.deliverable: A migration walkthrough and a list of unresolved governance decisions.

successCriteria: All ten selected records appear in the second application with original attribution, and no unselected resource becomes readable.
After revocation, the first client cannot perform new authorized reads or writes with its previous access.
Four of five participants correctly explain which data a client can currently access and which previously downloaded copies may remain.
nonGoals: Creating a universal reputation score or automatically granting membership
Guaranteeing erasure of copies already obtained by another party

challenges.title: Consent across contexts

blueprints.name: Shared writing that preserves disagreement
blueprints.line: Let drafts converge while keeping competing explanations visible.
blueprints.proposed: Extend a collaborative editor so independently edited passages retain authorship, competing alternatives, and review decisions when writers merge their offline work.
blueprints.opportunity: Extend a collaborative editor so independently edited passages retain authorship, competing alternatives, and review decisions when writers merge their offline work.
blueprints.existingWork: Peritext already implements a rich-text collaboration algorithm, an editor integration, demonstrations, and tests. This experiment explores editorial intent and review decisions around merged passages.

origin.title: Peritext: rich-text collaboration across independent drafts
origin.summary: Peritext studied how writers can edit independent rich-text drafts and later merge them while preserving formatting intentions. Its researchers described demand for private drafting and asynchronous collaboration, then developed an algorithm and prototype addressing concurrent text and formatting edits. The 2021 research article was revised for a 2022 CSCW publication.

history.summary: Peritext implemented rich-text merging across independent drafts. The proposed continuation gives writers a way to review the resulting arguments and preserve unresolved alternatives.
history.whatWasBuilt: The project supplies an algorithm, interactive demonstrations, editor integration, and tests. Its research focuses on inline rich-text behavior and explicitly separates the algorithm from a complete workflow, noting that version comparison interfaces were outside the presented system.
history.whatRemains: Develop a review layer that keeps competing explanations visible after drafts reunite. Writers should be able to accept a wording, keep two alternatives open, or record a disagreement without losing authorship. The merge supplies a common document state; an editorial decision supplies meaning and consent.

whyNow.summary: Our proposal targets groups writing research notes, technical recommendations, or collaborative explainers across different schedules. The existing prototype provides difficult text-merging behavior to study and reuse. A community can test whether explicit alternatives reduce pressure to accept an accidental merged wording, while measuring the extra review effort the interface creates.
beneficiaries: Technical communities preparing proposals with competing positions
Contributors who need time to draft privately before sharing

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Three writers independently revise a short technical proposal, then produce a reviewed edition that preserves five unresolved disagreements alongside its accepted text.

steps.title: Define the editorial record
steps.description: Give a proposed passage its author, source draft, rationale, and review state. Separate suggestions from direct edits and specify who may accept a change or mark an issue unresolved.
steps.deliverable: A compact proposal-and-decision model with worked editorial examples.

steps.title: Make private drafts rejoin visibly
steps.description: Show paragraph-level differences, formatting changes, and alternative passages before publishing. Preserve the original draft references so a writer can inspect what happened to their contribution after review.
steps.deliverable: A branch comparison and reunion screen.

steps.title: Keep disagreement attached to the text
steps.description: Allow an editor to retain alternatives, explain a chosen version, and reopen a decision when its paragraph changes. Ensure that rejecting a proposal does not rewrite what its author actually submitted.
steps.deliverable: A reviewed edition with inspectable alternatives and decision history.

steps.title: Evaluate a real writing cycle
steps.description: Recruit a small group with a genuine technical disagreement. Compare the reviewed edition with a simple automatically merged draft, asking each writer to identify accepted changes, unresolved points, and their own contribution.
steps.deliverable: A documented writing exercise and an anonymized comprehension study.

successCriteria: All three writers can recover the exact wording of their original submissions after the review cycle.
Readers correctly distinguish accepted text from all five seeded unresolved alternatives without consulting the authors.
Repeated synchronization in different orders preserves the same document and review records, including an edit that reopens a resolved issue.
nonGoals: Automatically judging the truth or quality of competing arguments
Implementing a complete desktop publishing system or silently resolving political disagreements

roles.contribution: Connect stable text positions with branch and review records.

roles.name: Editor or facilitator
roles.contribution: Design real review decisions and evaluate whether consent is represented accurately.

roles.name: Interaction designer
roles.contribution: Keep alternatives discoverable while preserving a readable main text.

challenges.title: Stable comments on changing passages
challenges.description: A disagreement can outlive the words that triggered it. Anchor review records to revisions and show when later edits have made their subject ambiguous.

challenges.title: Too much history can obscure reading
challenges.description: The document needs a clear accepted edition as well as a complete review record. Progressive disclosure should hide visual complexity without hiding that a dispute exists.

relatedWork.relationship: Existing rich-text merge research; the proposed contribution is an editorial review layer around its behavior.

blueprints.name: Small languages for everyday work
blueprints.line: Let a community describe its work in a language that fits what it does.
blueprints.proposed: Give a makerspace a simple language for workshop recipes, with live feedback, examples, and a visual trace explaining how each instruction is interpreted.
blueprints.opportunity: Give a makerspace a simple language for workshop recipes, with live feedback, examples, and a visual trace explaining how each instruction is interpreted.
blueprints.existingWork: Ohm already provides extensible grammars, separate semantic actions, and an interactive editor. Its documented applications include Seymour, Shadama, and turtle.audio. This proposal explores a community-owned language for workshop recipes.

origin.title: Ohm and modular language construction
origin.summary: Ohm's research contribution was to separate a language's grammar from the operations that give its sentences meaning. A grammar could support several interpretations, and either part could be extended independently. That makes a useful starting point for a community that wants to express recurring work in its own vocabulary: one workshop recipe could produce a checklist, a materials estimate, and an explanation of its steps.

history.summary: Ohm provides a working language toolkit. The proposed continuation helps a community maintain its own vocabulary, review language changes, and keep older recipes usable.
history.whatWasBuilt: Ohm already supplies grammar matching, separate semantics, browser use, an interactive editor, and textual and graphical parsing traces. Its documentation demonstrates arithmetic and other examples. These mechanisms can explain how text is recognized, but builders must still design the community's vocabulary and domain feedback.
history.whatRemains: Explore whether makerspace members can maintain their own recipe language over time: proposing a new instruction, seeing which old recipes it affects, and agreeing on a change without relying on the original developer. The experiment needs comprehensible errors and a shared change process as much as a parser.

whyNow.summary: Our proposal is to use an existing browser-capable toolkit to put more effort into participation and less into parser construction. Start with instructions for preparing a workshop, such as collecting materials and assigning tasks. A small, inspectable language could help groups preserve practical knowledge while making its interpretation visible to newcomers. This benefit remains a hypothesis to test with one community.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Five members can adapt ten workshop preparation recipes and explain the resulting checklist without editing JavaScript.

steps.title: Collect the community's examples
steps.description: Observe one recurring workshop and gather ten real preparation lists. Agree on five to eight instructions, expected results, and examples that should be rejected. Keep physical machine operation outside the language.
steps.deliverable: A reviewed vocabulary and example test collection.

steps.title: Make interpretation visible
steps.description: Implement the grammar and a checklist interpretation separately. Highlight the instruction behind each generated task; explain missing quantities and unknown names in workshop terms. Show a plain-language trace alongside the technical parse tree.
steps.deliverable: An editor with live checklist preview and understandable errors.

steps.title: Practice changing the language
steps.description: Let a member propose one new instruction and preview its effect on every example. Store recipe and grammar versions together, then run a second workshop using the changed version and record where members need help.
steps.deliverable: A versioned recipe library and a documented community change trial.

successCriteria: At least four of five participants correctly explain the output of three unfamiliar recipes.
All ten original recipes retain their expected output after an approved compatible change.
A member other than the developer publishes a recipe and corrects one error independently.
nonGoals: A universal programming language or automatic translation of unrestricted natural language.
Direct control of workshop machinery or certification that a procedure is safe.

roles.contribution: Collect examples and negotiate vocabulary with members.

roles.contribution: Implement grammar, interpretations, and compatibility checks.

challenges.title: A small language can grow into a maintenance burden
challenges.description: Require a real recurring example for each extension. Preserve a readable export and a migration path when vocabulary changes.

blueprints.name: Documents that become shared tools
blueprints.line: Let a useful document grow into an interactive tool as a group needs more from it.
blueprints.proposed: Start with a group's meeting document and let members turn part of it into an interactive decision board while preserving its history and shared editing.
blueprints.opportunity: Start with a group's meeting document and let members turn part of it into an interactive decision board while preserving its history and shared editing.
blueprints.existingWork: Webstrates already synchronizes persistent changes to web pages and explores software as computational media. Codestrates and Varv are related projects. This experiment focuses on a meeting document growing into a group's decision tool.

origin.title: Webstrates: Shareable Dynamic Media
origin.summary: Webstrates explored software in which documents and applications can change roles. A shared page can contain information, interaction, and computation, and its users can reshape these together. The vision matters when a group's ordinary notes acquire structure: a list of options might become a decision board without leaving the document that explains why those options exist.

history.summary: Webstrates was built and has supported further research. This entry proposes a focused community decision workflow within that broader direction.
history.whatWasBuilt: The platform persists changes to a web page and synchronizes them among clients. Codestrates subsequently combined prose and code with collaborative authoring and the ability to modify the environment itself.
history.whatRemains: Test whether a nontechnical group can promote selected meeting content into an interactive tool, revise the tool's rules, and later recover a readable explanation of a decision. Focus on who may change behavior, how changes are previewed, and what survives when a tool is removed.

whyNow.summary: Our proposed application is a decision document for a volunteer association choosing a small project. Starting from a functioning research platform lets a team test the difficult transition from writing together to changing behavior together. The hoped-for benefit is fewer disconnected copies of minutes, votes, and action lists, with the reasoning behind a decision still visible after a meeting.
beneficiaries: Facilitators supporting participants with different technical skills

buildPlan.firstMilestone: A five-person group turns its meeting options into a decision board, changes one rule, and exports a readable decision record.

steps.title: Begin with the meeting
steps.description: Use one group's actual agenda to define options, supporting arguments, and owners. Keep the first document readable without interactive elements, and assign stable identifiers so later transformations preserve links to the original discussion.
steps.deliverable: A shared meeting document with a plain-text export.

steps.title: Promote content into behavior
steps.description: Let a facilitator select the options and apply one reviewed decision-board template. Preview how choices are counted before activating it. Preserve the originating text and show which rule produced each result.
steps.deliverable: A reversible transformation from notes to a working decision board.

steps.title: Make changes accountable
steps.description: Separate editing the discussion from changing the counting rule. Save a version before each behavioral change, require a preview, and record the author and reason. Test recovery from a broken template with participants.
steps.deliverable: Version history, behavior permissions, and a demonstrated recovery path.

steps.title: Follow the next meeting
steps.description: Have the group reuse the document without its developer present. Observe whether participants can explain the result and distinguish later edits from the record of the original decision.
steps.deliverable: A reusable template and a report of observed failures.

successCriteria: All five participants find the original discussion behind a decision in under two minutes.
Changing a template preserves all written options and participant contributions.
A facilitator restores the previous working version without developer assistance.
nonGoals: A general replacement for office suites or a marketplace of arbitrary executable plugins.
Legally binding elections or formal governance guarantees.

roles.name: Interaction designer

challenges.title: Editing content and running code confer different powers
challenges.description: Use reviewed templates for the first trial. Give participants visible control over behavior changes and isolate executable content from account credentials.

challenges.title: History must retain meaning
challenges.description: A sequence of page mutations may not explain a decision. Save the relevant content, rule version, and outcome as a human-readable record.

blueprints.name: Automation recipes people can inspect
blueprints.line: Show people what an automation will read and change before it runs.
blueprints.proposed: Build a visual automation editor for community operations where every block declares the data it reads, the changes it makes, and the permissions it needs, with a preview before execution.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a visual automation editor for community operations where every block declares the data it reads, the changes it makes, and the permissions it needs, with a preview before execution.
blueprints.existingWork: Blockly already provides an extensible visual programming editor maintained by the Raspberry Pi Foundation. This experiment adds an understandable account of an automation's effects and permissions.

origin.title: Blockly and programming through a domain's own vocabulary
origin.summary: In their 2017 Blockly design paper, Pasternak, Fenichel, and Marshall explained that a block editor is only part of a programming system: each application must choose its own vocabulary, audience, and execution behavior. Blockly had already been released in 2012. The paper encouraged small, comprehensible sets of blocks rather than exposing every possible operation.

history.summary: Blockly provides an open-source editor for block-based programming and is maintained by the Raspberry Pi Foundation. The proposed continuation lets community organizers inspect an automation's effects before approving them.
history.whatWasBuilt: Blockly supplies customizable visual blocks, connections, and code generation. Its documentation makes clear that the application developer decides what the generated program does. The library alone does not define the community's permissions or the semantics of a safe preview.
history.whatRemains: Create a deliberately restricted language whose operations declare the records they read, the changes they request, and the authority they need. Connect those declarations to an enforceable execution model, rather than treating a human-readable description as a guarantee.

whyNow.summary: A community garden could start with a recipe that reads volunteer availability, identifies uncovered shifts, and prepares a draft schedule. Our hypothesis is that showing exact proposed changes would let more organizers inspect and maintain the recipe. Existing visual-editor components lower the cost of this focused experiment. Whether the preview is actually understood needs testing with organizers, including people who did not create the recipe.
beneficiaries: Members who inherit another person's automation

buildPlan.firstMilestone: An organizer builds and previews a recipe that proposes a draft rota from sample availability; another organizer accurately predicts its reads and writes.

steps.title: Define a small language
steps.description: Offer six operations covering reading availability, filtering, grouping, checking coverage, proposing assignments, and saving a draft. Specify input types, record scope, and effects for each operation.
steps.deliverable: A block vocabulary and executable examples for every operation.

steps.title: Make execution match the preview
steps.description: Evaluate recipes against a versioned snapshot. Display affected records and proposed changes. On approval, verify the inputs are unchanged and stop if the request exceeds the organizer's permissions.
steps.deliverable: A preview-to-approval flow with enforced permissions and stale-data handling.

steps.title: Share with evidence
steps.description: Package each recipe with sample inputs, expected outcomes, its author, and a change history. Ask a second group to adapt it, deliberately including missing availability and duplicate submissions.
steps.deliverable: Three inspectable recipes with reproducible demonstrations.

successCriteria: Four of five organizers identify all affected data categories and proposed write actions before running a recipe.
A changed input invalidates the preview and requires a fresh approval.
Rerunning an approved request never creates duplicate assignments.
nonGoals: Arbitrary JavaScript, unrestricted third-party connectors, or autonomous decision making.
Sending messages, making payments, or publishing schedules in the first milestone.

roles.name: Language designer
roles.contribution: Defines understandable blocks and precise effect semantics.

roles.name: Runtime developer
roles.contribution: Enforces record scopes, approvals, and repeat-safe execution.

roles.name: Community organizer
roles.contribution: Supplies real cases and tests whether another person can maintain the recipes.

challenges.title: Accurate declarations
challenges.description: A plugin that claims to read one field may execute broader code. Keep the initial runtime closed to arbitrary plugins and derive the preview from the same operations used to execute.

challenges.title: Changing reality
challenges.description: An accurate preview can become outdated before approval. Detect record changes, explain the conflict, and preserve a record of what the organizer actually approved.

relatedWork.relationship: Provides the existing editor foundation; the proposed permissions and preview behavior belong in the application built around it.

references.supports: Authorship, 2012 release history, audience-specific vocabulary, scope, and separation between editor and runtime.

references.supports: Current editor capabilities, application-defined behavior, and Raspberry Pi Foundation stewardship.

blueprints.name: A shared map of how a system might change
blueprints.line: Compare explanations of a system and see what follows from different assumptions.
blueprints.proposed: Let a group build a causal model, attach evidence and uncertainty to its connections, fork competing hypotheses, and compare what happens when an assumption changes.
blueprints.opportunity: Let a group build a causal model, attach evidence and uncertainty to its connections, fork competing hypotheses, and compare what happens when an assumption changes.
blueprints.existingWork: LOOPY already provides an interactive tool for thinking in systems. This proposal adds evidence, uncertainty, and a workflow for comparing competing models.

origin.title: LOOPY and conversations through simulations
origin.summary: Nicky Case released LOOPY in March 2017 to let people construct educational simulations by drawing. Its circles and arrows make feedback relationships interactive, while sharing and remixing let one person's model become the starting point for another's response. The underlying ambition is participatory systems thinking: people should be able to construct and challenge an explanation, rather than only consume one.

history.summary: LOOPY provides drawable, shareable simulations. The proposed continuation adds evidence to model relationships and lets groups compare competing explanations.
history.whatWasBuilt: The published tool supports interactive models, remixes, links, files, and embedding. Its examples span ecology and social feedback. These are accessible qualitative explanations; the appearance of an animated relationship does not establish that the modeled causal claim is true.
history.whatRemains: Add a workflow in which every important connection carries its rationale, evidence, and uncertainty, and two branches can be compared using the same starting scenario. A group should be able to preserve disagreement, including a missing connection, without forcing everyone into one supposedly authoritative diagram.

whyNow.summary: A repair collective could use this workshop tool to investigate why donated devices wait for repair. Members could compare explanations involving spare parts, volunteer availability, and intake practices, then decide which observations to collect. The aim is to make assumptions easier to discuss and test.
beneficiaries: Local groups trying to document competing explanations

buildPlan.firstMilestone: One group compares two explanations of a repair backlog and agrees on three observations that could distinguish them.

steps.title: Build a small shared model
steps.description: Limit the first diagram to eight variables. Give each a plain-language definition and distinguish measured observations from participants' assumptions. Record the time period and context to which the model is intended to apply.
steps.deliverable: A readable model and glossary reviewed by the participants.

steps.title: Attach reasons to connections
steps.description: Add evidence links, authorship, uncertainty notes, and a counterargument field to each relationship. Permit an explicitly unsupported hypothesis; avoid assigning numeric confidence unless the group can explain what that number means.
steps.deliverable: Inspectable relationship cards and an evidence export.

steps.title: Compare competing branches
steps.description: Fork a disputed model and replay the same qualitative input in both. Highlight which relationships differ and invite participants to write their expected outcome before running either branch.
steps.deliverable: A side-by-side comparison with recorded predictions.

steps.title: Turn uncertainty into a next action
steps.description: Run one facilitated session and select observations that would challenge each explanation. Revisit the diagrams after collecting those observations; retain the earlier versions and the reasons for revisions.
steps.deliverable: A revised model with a short record of what the group learned.

successCriteria: Every displayed relationship has an author, rationale, and explicit evidence or hypothesis label.
Participants can identify the changed assumptions between two branches without inspecting source code.
The group records at least three observations that could disconfirm its preferred explanation.
nonGoals: Quantitative forecasting, automatic causal discovery, or an official policy recommendation.
Ranking community members by the apparent correctness of their models.

challenges.title: Evidence can be selectively attached

blueprints.name: A neural network you can argue with
blueprints.line: Make a tiny neural network small enough to inspect and discuss together.
blueprints.proposed: Create a collaborative learning lab where people change a tiny neural network's inputs or weights, inspect the complete computation graph, and record competing explanations of its behavior.
blueprints.opportunity: Create a collaborative learning lab where people change a tiny neural network's inputs or weights, inspect the complete computation graph, and record competing explanations of its behavior.
blueprints.existingWork: micrograd already implements a small automatic differentiation engine and neural-network library. This experiment builds a shared learning experience around inspectable models and testable explanations.

origin.title: micrograd: learning from a complete small implementation
origin.summary: micrograd implements automatic differentiation over scalar operations and places a small neural-network library on top. Its small size makes the relationship between ordinary arithmetic, a computation graph, and backpropagation available for direct study. The educational direction is compelling: a learner can examine a complete working mechanism instead of treating training as a call to an opaque service.

history.summary: The engine, demonstration notebooks, and graph tracing already exist. The proposed addition is a shared investigation process around tiny models.
history.whatWasBuilt: micrograd's repository demonstrates binary classification and computation-graph tracing. TensorFlow Playground separately lets people change network settings and inspect neurons, weights, and training results in a browser.
history.whatRemains: Explore a classroom or study-group lab in which participants state a prediction, fork the same model, change one assumption, and compare reproducible results. Keep explanations next to the exact data, parameters, and training state they refer to, so disagreements can be tested rather than lost in a chat thread.

whyNow.summary: Our proposal is to make shared experimental habits the centerpiece of a compact learning tool. A small synthetic problem can keep every calculation available for inspection and avoid needing an external model API. The potential benefit is a stronger understanding of what a network actually computes and of the limits of an explanation based on a single successful run. Learning improvement must be measured, not assumed.
beneficiaries: Community study groups learning machine learning
Software builders seeking a concrete foundation before using larger libraries

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Four learners investigate one tiny classifier, reproduce each other's experiment, and trace one prediction and one gradient through the full graph.

steps.title: Make one run fully reproducible
steps.description: Use a small synthetic dataset and fixed initial parameters. Save input points, labels, model structure, learning rate, and update count in a portable experiment file. Include a reset that returns to exactly the same initial state.
steps.deliverable: A deterministic baseline with a downloadable experiment record.

steps.title: Expose arithmetic at two scales
steps.description: Let learners switch between the network diagram and its scalar operations. Show intermediate values and gradients, and link each selected operation to the corresponding implementation. Add numerical checks for the gradients on the teaching examples.
steps.deliverable: A traceable forward and backward pass with verified examples.

steps.title: Record predictions before changes
steps.description: Ask each learner to predict the effect of changing one weight, one mislabeled point, or the learning rate. Fork from the same saved state, run both branches, and attach a short explanation of where the prediction held or failed.
steps.deliverable: A shared comparison of hypotheses and reproducible outcomes.

steps.title: Test transfer of understanding
steps.description: Give learners a different tiny graph after the session. Ask them to explain a gradient and identify an experiment that would challenge their account of the classifier, without following the original walkthrough.
steps.deliverable: An anonymized learning evaluation and revised activities.

successCriteria: Imported experiment files reproduce the same outputs and update sequence within a documented numerical tolerance.
All teaching examples pass independent finite-difference gradient checks away from nondifferentiable points.
At least three of four learners explain an unfamiliar gradient path and propose a meaningful counterexperiment.
nonGoals: Training large models, interpreting commercial model internals, or predicting real people's attributes.
Claiming that a visible computation graph by itself establishes fairness or explains learned behavior completely.

roles.contribution: Design misconceptions, teaching examples, and learning evaluation.

roles.name: Numerical software developer
roles.contribution: Keep computation, gradient checks, and replay trustworthy.

challenges.description: Keep the initial graph deliberately small and reveal one path at a time. Preserve access to all operations without presenting them simultaneously.

challenges.title: A tidy demonstration can teach the wrong generalization
challenges.description: Include a failed prediction and an unstable training run. Separate observations about this saved experiment from claims about neural networks in general.

blueprints.name: Research trails another community can continue
blueprints.line: Pass on the reasoning behind a discovery, with branching paths through its evidence.
blueprints.proposed: Build a portable trail reader and editor where a community links passages, explains each connection, and hands a branching investigation to another group without losing attribution or uncertainty.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a portable trail reader and editor where a community links passages, explains each connection, and hands a branching investigation to another group without losing attribution or uncertainty.
blueprints.existingWork: Bush proposed transferable trails in the Memex essay. Hypothesis provides browser annotation. This experiment adds explicit reading order, reasons for connections, branching, and handoff between independently hosted communities.

origin.title: Memex and associative trails
origin.summary: As We May Think describes a personal information machine in which a reader connects records into named trails, adds side paths, and gives a trail to another person. Its enduring proposal is that a useful result includes the route through the evidence, allowing later readers to extend an investigation instead of starting over.

history.summary: Bush described a design vision in 1945. Later hypertext and annotation systems made linked reading and commentary practical. This continuation brings those capabilities together in a portable investigation that another community can extend.
history.whatWasBuilt: The modern Hypothesis client supports selecting passages and displaying annotations in browsers. Its source offers an annotation starting point, rather than a reconstruction of Bush’s device.
history.whatRemains: Make the reasoning path independently exportable, forkable, and repairable when sources change, then evaluate whether a new group can continue it accurately.

whyNow.summary: A community investigating an environmental question or maintaining a public-interest software project could preserve why it rejected one approach and pursued another. Browser annotations provide a practical starting point. The benefit to test is reduced rediscovery: a new participant should understand the evidence, alternatives, and unresolved questions before making another contribution.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Two groups exchange one twenty-source investigation, including three branches and one deliberately changed source, through an export file.

steps.title: Capture a reasoned connection
steps.description: Build a passage selector and trail editor. Each step records a source URL, an anchor, an author-written explanation, a date, and an optional next step. Let authors identify a connection as evidence, analogy, objection, or unresolved question.
steps.deliverable: A reader can follow a short investigation and inspect why each source was included.

steps.title: Make branching and handoff explicit
steps.description: Give trails stable identifiers and export their structure and original notes. A receiving group can fork a branch, add an objection, and compare its additions with the upstream trail while preserving the original attribution.
steps.deliverable: Two independent installations exchange a trail and distinguish original work from additions.

steps.title: Test what survives change
steps.description: Change a source document, withdraw a source, and remove access to another. Present an honest unavailable or uncertain anchor state. Ask unfamiliar readers to reconstruct the central claim using the remaining trail.
steps.deliverable: A published handoff exercise with recoverable anchors and a record of misunderstandings.

successCriteria: Every exported connection retains its source, explanation, and author.
Readers distinguish supporting evidence from objections without a facilitator.
A changed or missing source never silently appears as verified evidence.
nonGoals: Reproduce the mechanical Memex.
Copy full third-party papers into exports by default.
Automatically decide whether a research conclusion is true.

roles.contribution: Implement anchoring, navigation, and export.

roles.name: Research facilitator
roles.contribution: Design the reading task and observe misunderstandings.

roles.name: Community editor
roles.contribution: Create a useful first investigation with permissioned materials.

challenges.title: Trails can persuade by omission
challenges.description: An elegant path can conceal contradictory evidence. Make branches and excluded alternatives visible, and allow readers to annotate the framing of the investigation.

challenges.title: Evidence changes
challenges.description: A URL can survive while its content changes. Keep minimal anchors and version context, clearly separate unavailable content, and avoid presenting guessed matches as certain.

relatedWork.relationship: Existing annotation UI and anchoring to extend; it does not itself establish this trail handoff experiment.

blueprints.name: A shared link layer for documents you do not own
blueprints.line: Let communities connect manuals, reports, and web pages without changing the originals.
blueprints.proposed: Build a link service that lets a repair community maintain one set of explanatory connections across independently hosted HTML manuals and locally held documents.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a link service that lets a repair community maintain one set of explanatory connections across independently hosted HTML manuals and locally held documents.
blueprints.existingWork: Microcosm and other open hypermedia systems separated links from document content. The Open Hypermedia Protocol work addressed incompatible link services. Annotator already supplies web annotation components; the proposed contribution is a portable linkbase tested across two viewers.

origin.title: Microcosm and interoperable open hypermedia link services
origin.summary: The authors of Towards Interoperability in Open Hypermedia Linkservices described a concrete limitation: systems could keep links outside documents yet still require their own client protocols. They proposed a common model and protocol so viewers could cooperate with multiple services. This brief revives that interoperability question in a small, useful setting.

history.summary: Microcosm and other open hypermedia systems implemented external links in prototypes and commercial products. The Open Hypermedia Protocol addressed incompatible client interfaces. This continuation tests one shared link collection in two independently developed viewers.
history.whatWasBuilt: The paper describes Microcosm viewers and link-service communication scenarios. Annotator provides modern browser components for annotations, storage integration, and application permissions.
history.whatRemains: Separate link ownership from document ownership while preserving anchor meaning, contributor attribution, and the ability to switch link providers.

whyNow.summary: Repair groups often collect knowledge about materials they cannot edit: a manufacturer’s manual, a public service document, and their own troubleshooting note. A shared link layer could connect an ambiguous instruction to a community explanation. The initial value is measurable navigation between those materials, using owned or permissioned test documents and existing annotation components.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: One repair group maintains fifty links that work in an HTML viewer and a separate local-document viewer through the same exported linkbase.

steps.title: Define links as independent records
steps.description: Give each link its own identifier, endpoints, author, purpose, and visibility. Record enough anchor context to identify the target passage. Keep the link store independent from document storage, with an explicit policy for who may edit a link.
steps.deliverable: A small documented link format and a permissioned example collection.

steps.title: Build two different viewers
steps.description: Use Annotator for the HTML experience and implement a second adapter for a simple local text-document viewer. Both query the same service, show link purposes, and resolve endpoints without rewriting the underlying files.
steps.deliverable: A demonstration in which one link update becomes available in both viewers.

steps.title: Prove the exit path
steps.description: Export the collection and import it into a second service. Move a document and edit an anchor passage. Show broken or ambiguous targets for human repair, with a history of the correction.
steps.deliverable: A migration report showing which links survive, fail, or need review.

successCriteria: All unchanged test anchors resolve identically in both viewers.
Moving between services preserves link identity and authorship.
An unauthorized contributor cannot rewrite another group’s link collection.
nonGoals: Rewrite every existing desktop application.
Promise universal anchors for arbitrary file formats.
Republish copyrighted manuals as part of the link service.
