blueprints.name: Research maps that turn arrangement into useful structure
blueprints.line: Let a group organize uncertain evidence before it has agreed on the categories.
blueprints.proposed: Build a spatial research board that proposes collections from placement and appearance, asks people to confirm its interpretation, and preserves the original arrangement alongside a searchable structure.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a spatial research board that proposes collections from placement and appearance, asks people to confirm its interpretation, and preserves the original arrangement alongside a searchable structure.
blueprints.existingWork: VIKI was a working spatial hypertext system, and the preceding research developed heuristic recognition of implicit structure. Cytoscape.js supplies a graph interaction building block. This proposal concentrates on collaborative interpretation and reversible suggestions, rather than claiming to invent visual boards.

origin.title: VIKI and recognition of implicit spatial structure
origin.summary: VIKI explored how information organization emerges while people work. Semi-structured objects, spatial collections, and a parser allowed tentative visual arrangements to develop into more explicit types. Earlier research examined how proximity and visual conventions could reveal structure while acknowledging that human interaction was needed to guide interpretation.

history.summary: VIKI implemented spatial hypertext and recognition mechanisms. This continuation adds collaborative review of inferred relationships, so a group can preserve useful ambiguity while developing a shared interpretation.
history.whatWasBuilt: VIKI supported evolving objects, collections, composites, and spatial parsing. Cytoscape.js offers graph visualization and interaction code for a fresh implementation of the proposed board.
history.whatRemains: Test whether several people can refine inferred structure without erasing meaningful ambiguity or forcing everyone into one taxonomy.

whyNow.summary: A community comparing evidence about a local environmental problem may need to keep incomplete patterns visible before choosing labels. A board can hold conflicting explanations next to observations and let categories develop through use. Existing graph interaction code makes it feasible to test the difficult part: whether suggested structure helps participants explain their reasoning to each other.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: A group sorts sixty evidence cards, reviews suggested collections, and exports both the agreed structure and the unresolved spatial arrangement.

steps.title: Preserve an expressive board
steps.description: Build cards with source links, a short note, shape or label cues, and free placement. Support named regions without requiring every card to belong to one. Record moves so a group can return to a previous arrangement.
steps.deliverable: A board that supports incomplete, overlapping interpretations and reversible edits.

steps.title: Suggest structure with an explanation
steps.description: Start with inspectable rules for proximity, alignment, and repeated visual cues. Show the evidence behind a proposed collection and allow acceptance, rejection, or correction. Store inferred suggestions separately from relationships people explicitly create.
steps.deliverable: A suggestion panel whose decisions can be explained without a machine-learning model.

steps.title: Evaluate the handover
steps.description: Invite a second group to interpret the board and compare its understanding with the original group’s account. Export cards, coordinates, accepted relationships, and source URLs. Reimport the file and inspect whether meaning survives.
steps.deliverable: A small study and a portable board format with documented ambiguous cases.

successCriteria: Rejecting a suggestion leaves the underlying board unchanged.
An exported board retains unresolved cards and overlapping regions.
Participants can identify which relationships were inferred and which were authored.
nonGoals: Automatically discover the correct taxonomy.
Replace detailed source reading with card summaries.
Require a graph layout algorithm to decide where every card belongs.

roles.name: Interaction designer
roles.contribution: Design reversible suggestions and accessible board navigation.

roles.name: Frontend developer
roles.contribution: Implement cards, history, and export.

roles.name: Research facilitator
roles.contribution: Observe interpretation differences between groups.

challenges.title: Proximity has many meanings
challenges.description: A nearby card might be a counterexample, a reminder, or a temporary parking place. Suggestions must remain provisional and show the rule that produced them.

challenges.title: A canvas can exclude people
challenges.description: Provide a keyboard-accessible list and region outline with equivalent operations. Test whether the structured view communicates the same relationships as the spatial one.

blueprints.name: A community memory you can search through time
blueprints.line: Bring decisions, documents, and future commitments into a chronology that survives a change of tools.
blueprints.proposed: Build a community chronicle that imports permissioned records from several tools, preserves event time and provenance, and helps a newcomer reconstruct how one project decision unfolded.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a community chronicle that imports permissioned records from several tools, preserves event time and provenance, and helps a newcomer reconstruct how one project decision unfolded.
blueprints.existingWork: Yale’s Lifestreams prototype organized personal information as a time-ordered stream, and its authors describe later related commercial work. Tantivy supplies full-text search. This experiment focuses on a portable group history and understandable provenance.

origin.title: Lifestreams
origin.summary: The Yale project proposed organizing documents and electronic events in a time-ordered stream, including future reminders, with operators for finding, filtering, and summarizing information. Its project page describes personal-information prototypes and identifies enterprise information as a direction that the researchers were beginning to explore.

history.summary: Lifestreams produced a working personal-information prototype and related commercial efforts. This continuation applies its chronology and filtering model to a group history that remains reconstructable when the community changes tools.
history.whatWasBuilt: A research architecture, personal-information prototype, and related later efforts are documented by the authors. Tantivy supplies a modern full-text index and query implementation.
history.whatRemains: Give a group a reconstructable history whose dates, edits, imported records, and missing context remain understandable after a tool migration.

whyNow.summary: Volunteer teams change tools and participants over time. A project’s rationale can become difficult to reconstruct when an issue, a meeting note, and a later correction live apart. The experiment would help a new maintainer answer what changed and why. A local search library allows an initial test without sending a group’s entire history to an external search service.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Import three months of permissioned records from two sources and let a new participant reconstruct five decisions with their supporting documents.

steps.title: Model time honestly
steps.description: Define a record with event time, import time, source identifier, author, and revision relationship. Preserve original timestamps and distinguish scheduled commitments from completed events. Build importers for a simple issue export and Markdown meeting notes.
steps.deliverable: A deterministic import fixture with duplicates, edited records, and future reminders.

steps.title: Build chronology and focused search
steps.description: Index record text and metadata with Tantivy. Let people move from a search result into its surrounding chronology, save a query as a substream, and attach a concise explanation of a decision that links back to source records.
steps.deliverable: A usable chronology with source-aware search and editable decision summaries.

steps.title: Test migration and onboarding
steps.description: Export records and index-independent metadata, rebuild on a fresh machine, and replay the five decision tasks with newcomers. Include one removed source and a corrected date; observe whether readers recognize both limitations.
steps.deliverable: A repeatable migration and onboarding exercise with accuracy and time measurements.

successCriteria: Reimporting a source creates no duplicate events.
Every displayed event distinguishes source time from import time.
A newcomer can locate the evidence for a decision and its later correction.
nonGoals: Record every private communication automatically.
Treat chronology as proof of causation.
Require every community tool to adopt a single application or database.

roles.contribution: Design import, deduplication, and portable records.

roles.name: Search developer
roles.contribution: Build source-aware queries and chronology navigation.

roles.name: Community historian
roles.contribution: Select decisions and validate reconstruction tasks.

challenges.title: Chronology can create false confidence
challenges.description: Events close in time may be unrelated. Explanations should cite actual decision records and mark missing context rather than infer intent from sequence.

challenges.title: History includes people’s private information
challenges.description: Import only material the group is entitled to use. Design deletion, redaction, and permission changes before adding more connectors, including removal from search indexes.

blueprints.name: A personal knowledge graph with a deliberate sharing boundary
blueprints.line: Connect your documents and contacts while choosing exactly which relationships a group can see.
blueprints.proposed: Build a local semantic index that relates files, contacts, and project notes, then lets a member publish a previewable subset of those relationships to a community.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a local semantic index that relates files, contacts, and project notes, then lets a member publish a previewable subset of those relationships to a community.
blueprints.existingWork: NEPOMUK delivered an open-source framework and reference implementations for a social semantic desktop, including cross-application links and social exchange. RDFLib already handles RDF graphs. This proposal tests a specific, understandable sharing boundary rather than recreating the entire desktop.

origin.title: NEPOMUK: the Social Semantic Desktop
origin.summary: NEPOMUK aimed to connect personal information across applications and support exchange across social and organizational relationships. The project combined semantic data structures, adapters, and collaboration research. DFKI’s account describes both a delivered open-source framework and a broader ambition to make personal knowledge useful across workspaces.

history.summary: The framework and implementations existed. The proposed work isolates one question within that broad vision: can an ordinary participant understand and control the exact slice of personal context being shared?
history.whatWasBuilt: NEPOMUK produced cross-application infrastructure and reference implementations. RDFLib provides a later, separately licensed RDF representation, parsing, serialization, and query building block.
history.whatRemains: Build a human-readable sharing preview, provenance-aware relationship selection, and a revocation workflow that distinguishes local deletion from copies already received.

whyNow.summary: An open-source contributor may want to share relevant project context without publishing their personal address book or all files mentioning a collaborator. A small local graph could connect that information while keeping publication deliberate. The benefit to test is confident, limited knowledge exchange: users should understand what a recipient will learn, including implications from visible relationships.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Index a participant-created test folder and contact list, share ten selected relationships, and verify the recipient sees only the approved export.

steps.title: Build a small local graph
steps.description: Write opt-in adapters for Markdown files and a user-provided contacts file. Store facts with source provenance and stable identifiers. Keep inferred relationships separate from explicit ones, and allow a person to inspect and correct each connection.
steps.deliverable: A local browser for relationships with source-level explanations and no automatic upload.

steps.title: Design the publication preview
steps.description: Let a member select a project and inspect the exact entities, labels, and relationships that would leave their machine. Highlight references that reveal an otherwise hidden contact or document title. Generate a portable RDF export only after confirmation.
steps.deliverable: An export preview that matches the recipient’s imported view field for field.

steps.title: Exercise correction and withdrawal
steps.description: Share the export with a separate installation, correct a mistaken identity merge, and withdraw selected relationships. Represent subsequent correction requests explicitly, while explaining that a recipient may retain earlier copies.
steps.deliverable: A documented exchange protocol and a study of whether participants understand its boundaries.

successCriteria: Private source contents never appear in an export unless explicitly selected.
Every visible fact can be traced to its source or identified as an inference.
Participants accurately predict which contacts and document names a recipient will see.
nonGoals: Index the whole computer by default.
Promise to erase data from someone else’s offline copy.
Require collaborators to share their entire personal graph.

roles.name: Data developer
roles.contribution: Build adapters, identifiers, and export.

roles.name: Privacy-focused designer
roles.contribution: Test the sharing preview and withdrawal explanation.

roles.name: Community participant
roles.contribution: Supply a realistic consented information set and feedback.

challenges.title: Relationships reveal information indirectly
challenges.description: Even an innocent title or connection can identify a confidential collaborator. The preview must show the recipient’s complete resulting graph rather than a list of selected files.

challenges.title: Names do not establish identity
challenges.description: Two contacts may share a name, and one person may use several addresses. Keep suggested merges reversible and preserve the evidence for each identity decision.

blueprints.name: Views of public knowledge that communities can share
blueprints.line: Let a useful way of reading a dataset travel independently of the website that first displayed it.
blueprints.proposed: Build two independent data browsers that can import the same community-authored presentation lens and show a consistent, accessible view of a public-interest dataset.
blueprints.opportunity: Build two independent data browsers that can import the same community-authored presentation lens and show a consistent, accessible view of a public-interest dataset.
blueprints.existingWork: Fresnel defined a browser-independent RDF display vocabulary, and its project lists several implementations. N3.js handles RDF data in JavaScript. This experiment tests a small portable lens profile and community authoring across independent viewers.

origin.title: Fresnel display vocabulary
origin.summary: Fresnel separates which RDF properties a reader sees from how those properties are presented. Its authors wanted presentation knowledge to be reusable across browsers rather than reimplemented in each application. Lenses choose and order information; formats guide rendering. The specification explicitly allows different output formats and representation styles.

history.summary: Fresnel was implemented in browsers and APIs listed by its project. This continuation develops a small, community-maintained compatibility profile for accessible viewers, with examples that independent implementations can test.
history.whatWasBuilt: The vocabulary, manuals, and multiple historical implementations exist. N3.js supplies a modern RDF parser and store for implementing a new lens evaluator.
history.whatRemains: Let a non-specialist publish a useful reading view and prove that independent viewers preserve its field selection, labels, ordering, and limitations.

whyNow.summary: Community groups interpreting public datasets often need domain knowledge to decide which fields matter and how to explain them. Sharing that reading view could help another town or volunteer group reuse the work. The initial test should use a small dataset with explicit reuse permission and compare understanding across two interfaces, including an accessible text-oriented one.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Create one reusable lens for a community-owned dataset and render it in an interactive browser and a keyboard-first document view with identical selected information.

steps.title: Specify a modest profile
steps.description: Choose a documented subset: resource types, ordered properties, labels, simple nested records, and missing-value behavior. Write conformance examples with expected selections. Keep rendering rules declarative, with no executable code embedded in a lens.
steps.deliverable: A short compatibility profile and fixtures that both implementations can test.

steps.title: Build an authoring experience
steps.description: Use N3.js to read the underlying graph and develop a form-based editor for field selection and explanation. Preview records with missing and repeated values. Allow community authors to attach a version, authorship, license, and intended use to their lens.
steps.deliverable: An exportable lens that a domain volunteer can create without hand-editing RDF.

steps.title: Implement an independent reader
steps.description: Have a second contributor build the document renderer against the profile rather than the first viewer’s internals. Import the same lens and compare selected content, field order, and keyboard navigation on the test fixtures.
steps.deliverable: A cross-viewer demonstration and a published compatibility report.

successCriteria: Both viewers select the same facts for every profile fixture.
Unsupported features produce an explicit notice instead of silently changing meaning.
A volunteer can revise field labels and publish a new lens without changing application code.
nonGoals: Force identical pixels in every viewer.
Treat a presentation filter as access control.
Claim full Fresnel compatibility from a limited subset.

roles.contribution: Implement the profile and reference evaluator.

roles.name: Accessibility developer
roles.contribution: Build the independent document view.

roles.name: Domain volunteer
roles.contribution: Author explanations and check whether the selected facts are useful.

challenges.title: A polished view can hide missing data
challenges.description: The lens should explain absent and filtered properties. Readers need a way to inspect the underlying record so a selective presentation does not become a misleading completeness claim.

challenges.title: Compatibility is more than parsing
challenges.description: Two readers may interpret nested records or unsupported selectors differently. Use executable examples and visible version negotiation, and distinguish data selection from visual styling.

blueprints.name: Annotations that travel with their community
blueprints.line: Move a group’s conversation about evidence between services without detaching it from the passages.
blueprints.proposed: Build a portable annotation exchange that preserves passage anchors, authorship, reply context, and visibility when a reading group migrates to another independently hosted service.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a portable annotation exchange that preserves passage anchors, authorship, reply context, and visibility when a reading group migrates to another independently hosted service.
blueprints.existingWork: W3C Web Annotation is a published standard with an implementation report, and Hypothesis provides an annotation client. This proposal evaluates migration between services with explicit tests for reply context, attribution, visibility, and changed source material.

origin.title: Web Annotation and interoperable annotation collections
origin.summary: The Web Annotation Data Model describes a common representation for annotations, bodies, targets, and selected regions of resources. It aims to support sharing and migration across systems without losing significant information. Its implementation report documents working implementations, while the model distinguishes the representation from the transport used to exchange it.

history.summary: The standard and multiple applications are real. The proposed experiment takes the interoperability ambition into a practical community exit test with replies, access boundaries, and changing source material.
history.whatWasBuilt: The standardized model represents annotation bodies, targets, selected passages, and collections. The implementation report documents working applications, and the Hypothesis client provides browser-based selection and discussion interfaces.
history.whatRemains: Demonstrate understandable movement between independent services and show precisely which metadata, rights, and conversation structures survive.

whyNow.summary: A reading group should be able to change its hosting arrangement without losing months of discussion about evidence. An interoperable model and reusable client make a focused test possible. The social benefit is continuity and choice: participants should know who wrote an observation and which passage it addressed after the original service is gone.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Move one hundred permissioned annotations and a threaded discussion between two local services, then inspect changed documents and withdrawn memberships.

steps.title: Make an exchange profile
steps.description: Define exactly how the experiment represents annotations, creator attribution, replies, quote anchors, timestamps, and collection membership. Add an explicit visibility policy outside the data model where needed. Write fixtures covering edited and deleted annotations.
steps.deliverable: A documented export profile with expected import results and known limitations.

steps.title: Build two service adapters
steps.description: Adapt the Hypothesis client where appropriate and implement separate storage adapters. Keep exported creator attribution distinct from locally authenticated account identity. Show imported authors as attributed historical authors unless identity is independently verified.
steps.deliverable: A pair of installations that display the same imported discussion without granting impersonation rights.

steps.title: Test real migration failures
steps.description: Remove a group member, change a target passage, and import a collection twice. Check deduplication, inaccessible replies, uncertain anchors, and explicit withdrawal requests. Ask participants to verify what another member can actually see.
steps.deliverable: A migration checklist backed by fixtures and a participant walkthrough.

successCriteria: Export and reimport preserve all supported annotation fields and reply relationships.
Historical creator attribution cannot be used to log in as that person.
Private collections never become public through a default import choice.
nonGoals: Claim federation merely because two systems accept JSON.
Promise recall of every annotation copy already exported.
Treat the W3C data model as a complete authentication or moderation protocol.

roles.name: Interoperability developer
roles.contribution: Specify the exchange profile and adapters.

roles.name: Identity developer
roles.contribution: Separate account permissions from imported attribution.

roles.name: Community moderator
roles.contribution: Define visibility and withdrawal expectations with participants.

challenges.title: Attributed identity is not authenticated identity
challenges.description: Imported annotations can name anyone. Preserve the claim and its provenance, but do not infer account ownership or verification from an exported creator field.

challenges.title: Portability includes uncomfortable cases
challenges.description: Deletion, blocked members, and orphaned replies can change the meaning of a conversation. Show what cannot be preserved and provide a review screen before publishing imported material.

relatedWork.relationship: Evidence that annotation models were implemented; also shows variation in supported features.

blueprints.name: Small tools that gather around a shared task
blueprints.line: Bring the relevant people, notes, and actions together without making everyone move to one application.
blueprints.proposed: Build a task-oriented workbench where a community can assemble a contact view, evidence list, and next-action tool around shared records, with changes reflected across those tools.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a task-oriented workbench where a community can assemble a contact view, evidence list, and next-action tool around shared records, with changes reflected across those tools.
blueprints.existingWork: MIT’s Haystack was an implemented platform for RDF-based end-user applications, with customizable interfaces and cooperative tools. N3.js provides a modern RDF building block. The proposed contribution is a narrow community task kit with independently replaceable tools.

origin.title: Haystack and information-centric cooperative tools
origin.summary: Haystack explored interfaces where information objects could be managed across views instead of remaining trapped inside separate application models. Its researchers implemented an RDF-based platform and argued for small cooperative tools. They also treated user-interface specifications as structured data so applications could be extended and customized.

history.summary: Haystack existed as an extensible research platform. The proposed experiment revisits its cooperative-tool model with a specific community workflow and a measurable replacement test.
history.whatWasBuilt: The papers describe tools for creating, viewing, and manipulating RDF information, including direct manipulation of information objects. N3.js supplies a later parser and store for new browser-based tools.
history.whatRemains: Demonstrate that a group can replace one tool without losing shared records, breaking task context, or learning the underlying graph representation.

whyNow.summary: A volunteer group organizing a repair event might coordinate people, equipment, and preparation notes in several separate tools. A small shared information model could support focused views for each task while retaining coherent records. The benefit to test is fewer repeated updates and easier tool replacement, using one deliberately limited workflow rather than proposing a universal desktop.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Support planning one repair event through three small tools, then replace the contact tool with a separately written implementation without changing the event records.

steps.title: Choose one shared task model
steps.description: Define stable identifiers for events, people, equipment, and preparation actions. Record provenance and ownership for each editable field. Build a small permissioned dataset and explain it in domain language before writing the interface.
steps.deliverable: A documented task model and examples that organizers can understand and correct.

steps.title: Assemble three cooperative tools
steps.description: Use a common RDF store with a contact view, an equipment checklist, and an evidence-notes panel. Let an organizer move a person or item into a task context through direct manipulation or equivalent keyboard actions.
steps.deliverable: An event workbench where all three tools show consistent updates to the same records.

steps.title: Prove independent replaceability
steps.description: Have another contributor implement the contact view against documented records and operations. Export the event, open it with the new tool, and ask organizers to complete the same preparation scenario.
steps.deliverable: A replacement demonstration identifying any hidden assumptions between components.

successCriteria: Editing one shared record does not create competing copies in different tools.
The replacement tool completes the same agreed organizer tasks.
Organizers can use the workbench without understanding RDF syntax.
nonGoals: Rebuild all desktop applications.
Turn arbitrary imported data into trustworthy shared facts.
Execute unreviewed interface plugins with unrestricted access to group records.

blueprints.name: Document collections that follow the work
blueprints.line: Let the same document belong to several useful contexts, with understandable rules for what happens next.
blueprints.proposed: Build a property-based document organizer for a community project, where personal and group views coexist and simple rules propose actions without moving or duplicating the original files.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a property-based document organizer for a community project, where personal and group views coexist and simple rules propose actions without moving or duplicating the original files.
blueprints.existingWork: Xerox PARC’s Placeless Documents was a working prototype with user-specific and active properties. DuckDB provides a modern local query engine. The proposed experiment focuses on understandable, reversible document behavior for a small community.

origin.title: Placeless Documents
origin.summary: Placeless Documents explored organizing information through document properties instead of one fixed hierarchy. Properties could represent users’ different perspectives, while active properties could attach behavior to documents. The research describes an experimental infrastructure and applications, with later reflection on how people adapt the system to their working practices.

history.summary: Placeless Documents implemented a property-based infrastructure and explored it through applications. This continuation focuses on transparent rules and coexisting community views, with preview and undo for metadata changes.
history.whatWasBuilt: Placeless supported user-specific properties and active document services. DuckDB supplies a separate MIT-licensed engine for querying structured metadata in a new implementation.
history.whatRemains: Let ordinary group members understand why a document appears in a collection, preview an action rule, and reverse mistaken metadata changes without losing their own organization.

whyNow.summary: A community preparing a public-interest software release might need views for missing approvals, contributor instructions, and translated material. Those views can overlap without duplicating files. The experiment would test whether inspectable document properties and suggested actions reduce filing work while allowing members to retain personal organization alongside the group’s process.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Organize one hundred permissioned documents into three overlapping group views and personal views, then safely preview and undo one metadata rule.

steps.title: Keep files and perspectives separate
steps.description: Index document identifiers, locations, versions, and selected metadata. Store group properties separately from personal properties, with attribution. Use DuckDB queries to form collections while leaving the underlying files in place.
steps.deliverable: A local organizer where a document can appear in several views with no duplicate file.

steps.title: Explain collection membership
steps.description: Build a readable filter editor and show which properties caused each document to appear. Let a participant override their own view without rewriting group policy. Provide a list of documents with insufficient metadata rather than hiding them.
steps.deliverable: Three useful collections with per-document explanations and explicit missing-data states.

steps.title: Add previewable actions
steps.description: Implement one bounded rule, such as suggesting a review label when required metadata is present. Show the exact affected records before approval and preserve an undo log. Test with a changed file location and a deliberately incorrect property.
steps.deliverable: A reversible rule demonstration and a report of whether participants predict its effect.

successCriteria: One file can appear in multiple collections without copied content.
A participant can explain why a document is included or omitted.
An approved metadata change can be reversed without overwriting another member’s later change.
nonGoals: Run arbitrary code embedded in downloaded documents.
Replace the operating system’s file permissions.
Automatically rename, move, or delete original files.

roles.contribution: Design rule previews and membership explanations.

challenges.title: Automation must remain legible
challenges.description: A rule that changes hundreds of records can be hard to inspect. Begin with bounded metadata suggestions, explain the trigger, and test undo before permitting any external action.

blueprints.name: Lesson books you can open and reprogram
blueprints.line: Turn explanations, simulations, and editable models into one learning material that students can inspect and change.
blueprints.proposed: Build a small, freely buildable authoring shell around Boxer’s separated evaluator, starting with a lesson where learners change the model as well as its inputs.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a small, freely buildable authoring shell around Boxer’s separated evaluator, starting with a lesson where learners change the model as well as its inputs.

Its README supplies SBCL and ECL core test commands and an ECL shared-library route; the latter excludes repaint and redisplay. Building the traditional desktop binaries requires a professional LispWorks license.

origin.title: Boxer and computational literacy
origin.summary: Boxer treats computation as a medium for thinking and learning. Its nested boxes combine data, procedures, and representations, with the broader ambition of making computational literacy part of ordinary education. The present project describes Boxer Sunrise as a continuing reference implementation, so this is a living lineage rather than an invented lost system.

history.summary: A working educational environment exists; a portable learning medium that communities can maintain using entirely free build tools is a focused continuation.
history.whatWasBuilt: Boxer Sunrise provides a desktop environment and documented core extraction. Its README supplies SBCL and ECL core test commands and an ECL shared-library route; the latter excludes repaint and redisplay. Building the traditional desktop binaries requires a professional LispWorks license.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed experiment is a new lesson interface around that core, with explicit model inspection, portable files, and classroom sharing. The team would build the lesson interface and graphics integration, then contribute improvements to the continuing Boxer project. The first lesson should focus on opening and changing the model itself.

whyNow.summary: A learning activity can be more informative when a student can examine the assumptions behind its animation. The hypothesis to test is whether opening a small model helps learners explain cause and effect better than moving sliders alone. A free build route would also let teachers maintain their materials independently of one desktop vendor.
beneficiaries: Learners moving from running models to changing them
Community education groups maintaining their own tools

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Deliver one executable lesson about household energy use, with nested data boxes, two editable procedures, and a visible explanation of each assumption.

steps.title: Establish the free runtime
steps.description: Build the separated evaluator with SBCL or ECL, document missing primitives, and run a tiny arithmetic and list example without LispWorks. Keep this reproducible before adding a user interface.
steps.deliverable: A build recipe and a compatibility checklist.

steps.title: Make the model inspectable
steps.description: Write a new interface that opens a box, shows its inputs and procedure, and previews a change before accepting it. Support keyboard navigation and undo from the beginning.
steps.deliverable: An editable lesson using original graphics and text.

steps.title: Test transfer of understanding
steps.description: Ask learners to predict an outcome, modify an assumption, and explain an unexpected result. Have another teacher adapt the lesson from its exported file.
steps.deliverable: A classroom trial report and a reusable lesson package.

successCriteria: The lesson builds and runs without a paid compiler or runtime.
A learner can identify and change one model assumption without assistance.
A second teacher can reopen the exported lesson and preserve its behavior.
nonGoals: Recreating every historical Boxer primitive.
Replacing a school learning-management system.
Claiming the lesson is a validated energy forecasting tool.

blueprints.line: Make a bug report contain the input, code, and live intermediate results needed to understand it together.

blueprints.existingWork: Light Table shipped a customizable ClojureScript editor with inline evaluation, browser views, and language plugins. Its tutorial explains Python, JavaScript, and Clojure evaluation. Those capabilities provide the local observation model for a shareable explanation.

origin.title: Light Table’s inline feedback
origin.summary: Light Table explored an editor that displays evaluation results beside the code producing them. Its tutorial demonstrates inline values, stack traces, and connections to running language clients. The useful historical ambition is to keep the behavior of software close to the person trying to understand it.

history.summary: The inline editor was built; the project repository was archived in 2022. This proposal reuses that work for a specific collaborative debugging artifact.
history.whatWasBuilt: Light Table shipped a customizable ClojureScript editor with inline evaluation, browser views, and language plugins. Its tutorial explains Python, JavaScript, and Clojure evaluation. Those capabilities provide the local observation model for a shareable explanation.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed addition is a bounded debugging story: a pinned code revision, sanitized sample input, selected observations, and an explanation that a second builder can replay. The practical contribution is packaging selected observations into one reviewable artifact that works outside its author’s development session.

whyNow.summary: A maintainer often needs the path to an incorrect result, not just the final exception. A replayable explanation could make asynchronous help more useful across time zones and help new contributors learn a codebase. The question is whether a compact selected trace communicates better than a large console log without demanding a full live pairing session.
beneficiaries: Volunteer maintainers with limited pairing time
First-time contributors learning an unfamiliar codebase

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Create a local JavaScript demonstration where one builder records a failing data transformation and another replays the same observations from a GitHub-linked artifact.

steps.title: Define a portable record
steps.description: Store the source commit, runtime version, input fixture, observation locations, and expected outputs in a documented file. Treat explanatory prose and captured values as separate fields.
steps.deliverable: A versioned debugging-story format with two examples.

steps.title: Revive selected inline behavior
steps.description: Port or adapt the relevant MIT-licensed observation display into a maintained runtime. Execute pure sample functions in an isolated process with explicit time and memory bounds.
steps.deliverable: An editor showing values beside the observed expressions.

steps.title: Run an asynchronous repair exercise
steps.description: Give a second builder only the repository and the story. Record where replay fails, what information is missing, and whether their fix changes the observed result.
steps.deliverable: A reproducibility report and an improved sharing flow.

successCriteria: The second builder reproduces the same values without a private development environment.
Changing the source revision makes stale observations visibly stale.
The recorded artifact contains only selected fixture data, not ambient process state.
nonGoals: Recording every instruction of an arbitrary production service.
Uploading secrets or complete machine memory.
Restoring every Light Table plugin.

origin.title: Eve: computation for all
origin.summary: Eve proposed making records and reactive rules the common language of an application, including its interface and diagnostic information. The project’s roadmap separated an implemented programming environment from later distributed-computing and end-user-computing ambitions. Its inspector demonstrated connecting a visible outcome to the rules and data behind it.

history.summary: An early language and environment were implemented; the maintainers describe the v0.3 preview as no longer actively developed.
history.whatWasBuilt: The repository contains an Apache-licensed alpha language implementation. The project site demonstrates reactive record queries, interface generation, and inspection. It labels the later world-scale computer and computation-for-all milestones as designs, research, or prototypes.
history.whatRemains: The proposed continuation is deliberately smaller: a tool-lending group can inspect how availability and volunteer assignments were derived. Modern permission handling, durable storage, explanations of missing results, and a safe rule-editing workflow would need to be built and evaluated.

whyNow.summary: Small groups often encode their working rules in a spreadsheet or in one organizer’s memory. An explainable application could make those rules discussable when they produce an unfair or surprising outcome. This is a product hypothesis: the group should decide whether rule inspection is useful before the team attempts a general-purpose programming platform.
beneficiaries: Organizers who currently maintain informal spreadsheets

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Build a local tool-lending demonstration where every availability result can show the reservations and rules that produced it, using invented member data.

steps.title: Recover the rule engine
steps.description: Run the pinned alpha’s examples, document incompatible dependencies, and implement a small lending schema using records. Keep external effects out of the first model.

steps.title: Explain an outcome
steps.description: Select a visible result and display its supporting records and rule. Add a contrasting explanation for an unavailable item, including the exact reservation or missing requirement.
steps.deliverable: Two traceable explanations with links back to editable rules.

steps.title: Let the group propose a change
steps.description: Preview a new lending limit against saved examples before accepting it. Record who approved the rule and which outcomes changed. Include conflicting proposals from two organizers so the interface has to explain disagreements instead of silently taking the newest edit.
steps.deliverable: A rule review screen and before/after examples.

successCriteria: Every shown availability result can be traced to the records used.
A rule change previews its effects without mutating real reservations.
An organizer can explain one unexpected decision without reading the entire program.
nonGoals: Automating consequential eligibility decisions.
Building the full distributed Eve roadmap.
Assuming provenance alone makes a decision fair.

blueprints.name: A shared library of methods that keeps its meaning
blueprints.line: Let communities reuse a calculation by its exact definition, even when names, projects, and maintainers change.
blueprints.proposed: Build a small methods library on Unison’s content-addressed code, with worked examples, provenance, and an explicit review path for updated definitions.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a small methods library on Unison’s content-addressed code, with worked examples, provenance, and an explicit review path for updated definitions.
blueprints.existingWork: The language already supports content-addressed definitions, type-aware tools, and persistent codebase storage. Unison Share already publishes browsable libraries. The proposed library would use those existing capabilities to organize domain review and long-lived calculation records.

origin.title: Unison’s content-addressed codebase
origin.summary: Unison identifies a definition by a hash of its syntax tree rather than by a mutable name. References include the identities of dependencies, and human-readable names are stored separately. That design makes software a structured body of reusable definitions rather than only a collection of text files.

history.summary: Unison is a real, continuing language with a codebase manager, library-sharing ecosystem, and commercial cloud platform. This entry proposes a community application of those foundations.
history.whatWasBuilt: The language already supports content-addressed definitions, type-aware tools, and persistent codebase storage. Unison Share already publishes browsable libraries. The proposed library would use those existing capabilities to organize domain review and long-lived calculation records.
history.whatRemains: Our experiment is a narrowly curated library of public-interest calculation methods: each definition carries a worked example, domain assumptions, a reviewer, and a migration explanation. The team would test that review workflow with contributors who need to distinguish changed methods from changed data.

whyNow.summary: A reproducible method needs more than a familiar function name. Communities comparing a calculation over time need to know whether its definition or its inputs changed. Content-addressed references could preserve that distinction while ordinary names remain readable. A pilot can test whether this reduces accidental drift when several groups adapt the same method.
beneficiaries: Maintainers of small public-interest software libraries

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Publish ten simple, originally authored methods for processing community survey data, with pinned definitions, synthetic inputs, expected results, and explicit assumptions.

steps.title: Model a complete method record
steps.description: Attach a definition hash, input and output types, license, units, sample cases, and limitations to each method. Include a deliberately changed denominator to make version differences visible.
steps.deliverable: A documented record format and ten licensed examples.

steps.title: Build a reviewable update path
steps.description: Show two method versions side by side with changed dependencies and rerun examples. Let a downstream project accept an update deliberately while retaining its previous definition.
steps.deliverable: A prototype method browser and update comparison.

steps.title: Test reuse across groups
steps.description: Have two groups calculate the same synthetic survey summary independently, then change one method. Check that both can explain why old and new results differ.
steps.deliverable: A reproducibility exercise with an exported evidence bundle.

successCriteria: Reopening a saved analysis resolves the exact same definition and dependencies.
Renaming a method does not change its identity or result.
An update shows changed assumptions and examples before it is accepted.
nonGoals: Duplicating the full Unison Share service.
Treating a hash as proof that a method is scientifically valid.
Depending on paid cloud hosting for the pilot.

blueprints.name: A portable view of the resources a task needs
blueprints.line: Give a project one inspectable resource tree for its data and tools, regardless of where those resources live.
blueprints.proposed: Adapt Plan 9’s per-process namespace idea into a task launcher that exposes only selected project resources and makes their origins visible.
blueprints.opportunity: Adapt Plan 9’s per-process namespace idea into a task launcher that exposes only selected project resources and makes their origins visible.
blueprints.existingWork: Plan 9 supplied namespace assembly and remote file-like services. The 9fans Go repository provides packages for interacting with Plan 9 and ports of libraries and tools. It is a reusable implementation foundation, not a full task launcher.

origin.title: The Use of Name Spaces in Plan 9
origin.summary: The Plan 9 paper describes a distributed operating system built around per-process namespaces and a common file protocol. A process assembles its own view of local and remote resources rather than relying on one global arrangement. This provides a concrete historical model for making a task’s dependencies explicit and rearrangeable.

history.summary: Plan 9 implemented this architecture. The opportunity here is a modern task-level application for community projects using existing operating systems.
history.whatWasBuilt: Plan 9 supplied namespace assembly and remote file-like services. The 9fans Go repository provides packages for interacting with Plan 9 and ports of libraries and tools. It is a reusable implementation foundation, not a full task launcher.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed extension is an inspectable manifest that maps named task inputs to local files, read-only remote data, or small service adapters. It would show permissions and provenance before launch. A small pilot would focus on whether contributors can inspect and replace each resource mapping without modifying the task itself.

whyNow.summary: Volunteer projects may pass scripts between people whose data paths, credentials, and machines differ. A visible resource map could reduce hidden setup assumptions and make a copied task easier to understand. The pilot should test this benefit with harmless read-only inputs before attempting writable remote services or broad operating-system integration.
beneficiaries: Community data teams sharing repeatable tasks

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Create a local launcher for one report task that reads a synthetic CSV and a project configuration through a named resource tree, then writes to an isolated output directory.

steps.title: Specify the resource manifest
steps.description: Describe each resource’s logical path, origin, access mode, expected format, and freshness. Reject undeclared paths and keep secrets outside the shareable manifest.
steps.deliverable: A manifest specification with three complete task examples.

steps.title: Implement a narrow adapter
steps.description: Use the MIT-licensed protocol packages for a small resource service and client. Support read-only files first, log access attempts, and make unavailable resources fail clearly.
steps.deliverable: A working Go adapter and task launcher.

steps.title: Check portability and boundaries
steps.description: Run the task from two machines with different physical file layouts. Attempt access to a resource outside the declared tree and verify that the launcher and host isolation reject it.
steps.deliverable: A portability demonstration and boundary-test report.

successCriteria: The same logical manifest works with different local source paths.
The user can inspect each resource’s real origin and access mode.
An undeclared resource cannot be read through the task’s resource interface.
nonGoals: Replacing the host operating system.
Treating a namespace alone as a security sandbox.
Exposing an unauthenticated 9P service to the public internet.

challenges.description: A remote service may have costs, latency, and side effects unlike a local file. The first interface should make those differences visible rather than promise complete transparency.

blueprints.name: A computer you can understand from end to end
blueprints.line: Follow a small program through its compiler, memory, operating system, and display inside an explorable software lab.
blueprints.proposed: Build an annotated systems-learning layer around Project Oberon’s browser emulator, with traceable experiments connecting visible behavior to the corresponding source.
blueprints.opportunity: Build an annotated systems-learning layer around Project Oberon’s browser emulator, with traceable experiments connecting visible behavior to the corresponding source.
blueprints.existingWork: Wirth’s project page publishes book chapters, operating-system modules, compiler modules, applications, and hardware source. Michael Schierl’s emulator runs Project Oberon in JavaScript and Java and includes the source and tools used for its disk images.

origin.title: Project Oberon
origin.summary: Project Oberon set out to describe an entire implemented computing system clearly enough to understand it as a whole. Its book connects the operating system, compiler, and computer design. The revised 2013 edition moved the system to an FPGA-based RISC machine; the surviving source provides an unusually concrete basis for studying the complete stack.

history.summary: The complete system was built and documented. Browser and Java emulators also exist, so this proposal concerns explanation and experimentation around them.
history.whatWasBuilt: Wirth’s project page publishes book chapters, operating-system modules, compiler modules, applications, and hardware source. Michael Schierl’s emulator runs Project Oberon in JavaScript and Java and includes the source and tools used for its disk images.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed continuation is a guided lab that connects an action on screen to the exact modules and machine state involved. Learners would make a small system change, predict its effects, and compare a trace before and after. The team would develop that teaching layer with educators and compare its usefulness with running the existing emulator alongside the book.

whyNow.summary: A modern software stack can be too large for a beginner to inspect as one object. A small working system offers a different teaching scale: learners can follow a real path without replacing every component with a diagram. Browser access may reduce installation friction, while saved emulator states could support repeatable lessons and collaborative investigation.
beneficiaries: Students learning operating systems and compilers
Builders interested in comprehensible computing infrastructure

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Produce one lesson that follows a text-rendering operation from an Oberon command through the display code to a visible pixel change.

steps.title: Pin an inspectable system
steps.description: Choose one emulator revision and disk image, inventory the included licenses, and link the image’s modules to their exact source versions. Avoid mixing source and binaries from different releases.
steps.deliverable: A reproducible lesson image and source map.

steps.title: Add selected observation points
steps.description: Expose relevant registers, memory locations, and module calls at a few points in the rendering path. Explain why each observation matters and allow the learner to step or reset.
steps.deliverable: A browser lesson with a short annotated trace.

steps.title: Make and explain a change
steps.description: Ask learners to alter a small display behavior, rebuild the affected module, and predict the difference. Have a second learner reproduce the result from the saved experiment.
steps.deliverable: A documented modification exercise and learner feedback.

successCriteria: Every displayed code reference resolves to the version running in the emulator.
A learner can explain the path from command to display change.
Resetting the lesson restores a known state and reproduces its trace.
nonGoals: Rewriting Oberon’s compiler or operating system.
Replacing a modern secure desktop.
Building new FPGA hardware for the first milestone.

roles.contribution: Expose deterministic observation and reset controls.

roles.name: Systems teacher
roles.contribution: Choose a path that spans layers without overwhelming learners.

roles.name: Technical illustrator
roles.contribution: Make the source and machine-state relationships legible.

challenges.title: Small does not mean familiar
challenges.description: Oberon’s interaction conventions can distract learners. Teach only the commands needed for the experiment and provide a readable alternative to mouse chords.

challenges.title: Instrumentation changes timing
challenges.description: Tracing can alter execution speed. Separate functional observations from performance claims and document any emulator-specific behavior.

blueprints.name: One program, several human languages
blueprints.line: Let collaborators view the same structured program using names and explanations in the language they understand best.
blueprints.proposed: Extend Lamdu’s existing internationalized code display with a community-maintained vocabulary and lessons that test collaboration across languages.
blueprints.opportunity: Extend Lamdu’s existing internationalized code display with a community-maintained vocabulary and lessons that test collaboration across languages.
blueprints.existingWork: Lamdu has a GPL-licensed implementation, downloadable releases, live evaluation, structure-aware editing, and existing translations. The project page credits Italian and Spanish translation contributors. Those translations provide concrete examples for contributors extending the shared vocabulary.

origin.title: Lamdu’s live structured programming environment
origin.summary: Lamdu explores editing a program as structure while retaining a familiar text-like interface. Its project page presents automatic layout, continuous evaluation, friendly type feedback, and internationalization that makes the human language of code a display choice. The declared goal is a complete programming language and environment; the current release is described as a technology preview.

history.summary: The structural editor and internationalization are already implemented. The project explicitly invites work on localization and documentation.
history.whatWasBuilt: Lamdu has a GPL-licensed implementation, downloadable releases, live evaluation, structure-aware editing, and existing translations. The project page credits Italian and Spanish translation contributors. Those translations provide concrete examples for contributors extending the shared vocabulary.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed experiment is a bilingual learning and collaboration package: shared examples, a curated vocabulary, translation review, and a way to discuss one underlying definition across two displayed languages. The team would test whether a stable shared vocabulary improves learning and collaboration across the two displayed languages.

whyNow.summary: English terminology can add a second learning task when someone is first encountering programming concepts. Keeping program identity separate from display language could let a learner start with familiar words while an experienced collaborator sees another vocabulary. The goal is shared understanding, including an easy path to conventional technical terminology, rather than isolating language communities.
beneficiaries: Programming learners studying in a language other than English
Bilingual teachers and community coding clubs
Teams evaluating more accessible programming environments

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Create an English/Spanish lesson package with twenty shared definitions and a paired exercise that two people can complete while using different display languages.

steps.title: Build a reviewed vocabulary
steps.description: Choose a small domain such as household budgeting with fictional data. Record each concept’s identifier, display names, explanation, and examples; have both a language reviewer and a programming teacher check it.
steps.deliverable: A compatibly licensed bilingual vocabulary and lesson text.

steps.title: Keep discussions tied to identity
steps.description: Prototype references from a lesson comment to the underlying definition rather than its displayed spelling. Show the partner’s displayed name when useful without changing the program.
steps.deliverable: A paired lesson interface with stable definition references.

steps.title: Evaluate mixed-language work
steps.description: Ask pairs to locate a mistake, explain the relevant function, and make a shared change. Compare with the same lesson using one fixed vocabulary, recording confusion as well as completion.
steps.deliverable: A small study report and concrete localization fixes.

successCriteria: Switching display language leaves program behavior and definition references unchanged.
Both participants can find a referenced definition using their chosen vocabulary.
Reviewers can identify the source and license of every contributed translation.
nonGoals: Automatically translating and publishing unreviewed terminology.
Adding every spoken language in the first release.
Replacing interoperability with mainstream language ecosystems.

challenges.title: Translation is conceptual work
challenges.description: Literal substitutions may obscure technical meaning or introduce inconsistent names. Treat the vocabulary as reviewed content with examples and change history.

challenges.title: Sharing with text-based tools
challenges.description: Screenshots and copied text may lose structural identity. Provide readable exports that include stable references and the language used for display.

blueprints.name: Public data workflows people can inspect
blueprints.line: Make a community dataset’s cleaning steps visible as a runnable flow, with examples and explanations at each connection.
blueprints.proposed: Use NoFlo to create a small public-interest data pipeline whose transformations can be inspected, replayed, and maintained by several contributors.
blueprints.opportunity: Use NoFlo to create a small public-interest data pipeline whose transformations can be inspected, replayed, and maintained by several contributors.
blueprints.existingWork: NoFlo runs JavaScript components in connected graphs on Node.js or in a browser. Its ecosystem includes an editor, testing tools, and tracing tools. The existing library is a foundation for coordinating transformations, rather than a complete civic data product.

origin.title: Flow-Based Programming
origin.summary: Morrison’s Flow-Based Programming describes applications as networks of processes connected by information packets, with the connections separate from component internals. NoFlo brings a related model to JavaScript. Morrison’s own site distinguishes classical FBP from FBP-inspired systems, so this brief does not treat every visual graph runtime as implementing the same semantics.

history.summary: Flow-based programming, NoFlo, and graphical editors have all been built. The proposed work concerns a specific inspectable community workflow.
history.whatWasBuilt: NoFlo runs JavaScript components in connected graphs on Node.js or in a browser. Its ecosystem includes an editor, testing tools, and tracing tools. The existing library is a foundation for coordinating transformations, rather than a complete civic data product.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed continuation is a small workflow package that combines a graph with example records, explicit quality checks, transformation explanations, and reproducible releases. The pilot would test whether contributors can explain and repair a transformation by following one record through the graph.

whyNow.summary: Community data projects need more than a final CSV: another volunteer must understand why records were removed, grouped, or corrected. A visible flow can make those choices discussable, but a graph can also become unreadable. Start with a small dataset and measure whether contributors can explain and repair it before expanding into a general automation platform.
beneficiaries: Small organizations maintaining a shared directory

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Build a six-step pipeline for a fictional public-facilities directory: import, normalize fields, validate coordinates, identify duplicates, review corrections, and export.

steps.title: Design observable components
steps.description: Give each transformation a clear input schema, output schema, sample record, and failure channel. Preserve original values when applying a correction so the decision can be inspected later.
steps.deliverable: Six original MIT-licensed components with example fixtures.

steps.title: Make data movement inspectable
steps.description: Show a selected record before and after every step, including the reason for rejection or modification. Keep a concise text explanation alongside the graph for keyboard and screen-reader use.
steps.deliverable: A runnable graph with record-level inspection.

steps.title: Reproduce and review a release
steps.description: Pin graph and component versions, publish the input fixture and checksums, and have another contributor reproduce the exported directory. Review one changed transformation before accepting it.
steps.deliverable: A repeatable release recipe and a contributor trial.

successCriteria: Every output field and discarded record has an inspectable transformation history.
A second contributor reproduces the same export from the documented inputs.
An invalid input follows a visible error path instead of disappearing.
nonGoals: Building a universal no-code platform.
Replacing a data steward’s review of corrections.
Automatically publishing corrections without human review.

blueprints.name: Useful results while an analysis is still unfinished
blueprints.line: Let a group explore a calculation together while incomplete or conflicting parts remain visible instead of stopping the whole document.
blueprints.proposed: Build a small shared analysis lesson using Hazel’s typed holes, explicitly separating complete results from the results that depend on unfinished work.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a small shared analysis lesson using Hazel’s typed holes, explicitly separating complete results from the results that depend on unfinished work.
blueprints.existingWork: The web environment already evaluates incomplete programs and supports rich interactive constructs. The project lists collaborative-editing research and, in 2026, work on live typed tables. The lesson can build on those advances while giving participants a smaller, concrete collaboration task.

origin.title: Semantic foundations for editors and live collaborative computation
origin.summary: Hazel’s research program gives incomplete programs a defined meaning through typed holes. A missing or erroneous expression can remain a visible part of the program while completed portions still produce useful results. Later work proposed a live, rich, collaborative environment for planetary computation, linking this language foundation to shared scientific analysis.

history.summary: Hazel is an implemented, actively researched environment. The broader planetary-computation paper presents a vision and mockup rather than a delivered global platform.
history.whatWasBuilt: The web environment already evaluates incomplete programs and supports rich interactive constructs. The project lists collaborative-editing research and, in 2026, work on live typed tables. The lesson can build on those advances while giving participants a smaller, concrete collaboration task.
history.whatRemains: Our proposed experiment is a small shared lesson where two contributors compare alternative methods, leave a calculation unfinished, and still inspect independent results. The new product work includes a clear status vocabulary, an evidence trail for each result, and a collaboration trial; it does not require completing the entire research roadmap.

whyNow.summary: Exploratory analysis is often unfinished for good reasons: a method is disputed, data is missing, or a collaborator is testing an alternative. Keeping that uncertainty inside the computational object could make collaboration more honest. The pilot should test whether participants understand which results remain valid, rather than assuming continuous execution automatically improves scientific reasoning.
beneficiaries: Teachers demonstrating partial understanding and revision
Software teams exploring meaningful incomplete programs

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Create a browser lesson comparing two ways of summarizing a synthetic air-quality table, where an unfinished method leaves the independent summary usable and visibly identifies dependent results.

steps.title: Define partial-result behavior
steps.description: Start from Hazel’s existing holes and table capabilities. Specify how the lesson labels complete, incomplete, erroneous, and stale data without treating a hole as zero or an empty value.
steps.deliverable: A worked model with explicit result states.

steps.title: Make alternatives discussable
steps.description: Let contributors name two proposed methods, attach assumptions, and trace each output to the chosen definition and input revision. Preserve unresolved work rather than silently selecting a winner.
steps.deliverable: A comparison view with traceable alternatives.

steps.title: Evaluate interpretation
steps.description: Ask pairs to make a change, identify unaffected results, and explain what cannot yet be concluded. Check their answers against a deliberately incomplete reference analysis.
steps.deliverable: A user-study report focused on mistaken certainty and collaboration.

successCriteria: A missing expression never appears as a valid numeric result.
Independent outputs remain usable when another branch is incomplete.
Participants can identify which conclusions depend on unfinished work.
nonGoals: Producing validated air-quality advice.
Building a planetary-scale compute service.
Supporting every concurrent editing and merge scenario in the first release.

blueprints.name: Messages that travel when the network cannot
blueprints.line: Keep non-urgent community notices moving through temporary connections and volunteer relay points.
blueprints.proposed: Build a community notice service that stores messages until another device can carry them onward, with honest delivery status, expiry, and receipts that survive an interrupted connection.
blueprints.opportunity: Build a community notice service that stores messages until another device can carry them onward, with honest delivery status, expiry, and receipts that survive an interrupted connection.
blueprints.existingWork: The Bundle Protocol has multiple implementations. dtn7-rs provides a BP7 daemon, routing strategies, command-line tools, network discovery, and application interfaces. The transport can therefore be reused for the notice service.

origin.title: Delay-Tolerant Networking Architecture
origin.summary: The DTN architecture treats interruptions as a normal property of a network. A device retains a complete message and forwards it when a suitable contact appears, instead of requiring a continuous path between sender and recipient. RFC 4838 documents this store-and-forward architecture; Bundle Protocol version 7 later standardized its message format.

history.summary: DTN is implemented and standardized. The opportunity is an understandable, community-operated notice service built on that foundation.
history.whatWasBuilt: The Bundle Protocol has multiple implementations. dtn7-rs provides a BP7 daemon, routing strategies, command-line tools, network discovery, and application interfaces. The transport can therefore be reused for the notice service.
history.whatRemains: This proposal adds a complete experience for composing, relaying, expiring, acknowledging, and correcting ordinary notices. A sender needs to distinguish stored locally, copied to a relay, received by a destination, and actually acknowledged; those states should remain intelligible after several disconnected hops.

whyNow.summary: A library, traveling workshop, or rural association could test whether scheduled encounters make useful communications possible with fewer assumptions about connectivity. The proposed benefit is continuity for low-urgency coordination. It must be demonstrated through delivery trials rather than inferred from a successful network demo.

buildPlan.firstMilestone: Deliver 100 numbered test notices between three isolated local networks through one periodically connected relay, then reconcile receipts.

steps.title: Make the interruption visible
steps.description: Build a local outbox and inbox above dtn7-rs. Give every notice an identifier, destination, expiry, size limit, and status explanation that remains readable without a connection.
steps.deliverable: A working notice composer with a durable queue.

steps.title: Exercise scheduled encounters
steps.description: Connect relay nodes on a fixed schedule, deliberately interrupt transfers, and record which notices arrived, expired, or were duplicated. Compare routing settings with the same replayable contact pattern.
steps.deliverable: A reproducible three-network delivery experiment.

steps.title: Test the human handoff
steps.description: Ask volunteers to operate relays without a developer. Add clear storage limits, contact summaries, and a recovery procedure for a lost or full device.
steps.deliverable: An operator guide and usability report with delivery measurements.

successCriteria: Every received notice maps to a single original despite duplicate transport.
Expired notices are marked clearly and never presented as current.
Volunteers can explain the difference between relayed and acknowledged without assistance.
nonGoals: Emergency dispatch or guaranteed delivery
New radio hardware or replacement of the Bundle Protocol

roles.name: Network engineer
roles.contribution: Build the contact schedule and instrument transport behavior.

roles.name: Application developer
roles.contribution: Implement message state, receipts, and recovery.

roles.name: Community organizer
roles.contribution: Choose realistic notices and evaluate volunteer operation.

challenges.title: Delivery is not guaranteed
challenges.description: BP7 does not itself promise end-to-end arrival. Application receipts, expiry, and an explicit unknown state are essential; a green icon must not imply that a person has read a notice.

challenges.title: Relay trust and storage
challenges.description: A relay can withhold messages or run out of space. Begin with synthetic, non-sensitive notices and known operators; define authentication, retention, and abuse limits before handling real community information.

relatedWork.relationship: The existing transport standard this application would use, including its explicit delivery limitations.
